## Market Leader - Phosphoric Acid Market

* [DOWNLOAD PDF](/pdfdownloadNew.asp?id=177852938)

The phosphoric acid market is anticipated to grow from USD 112.03 billion in 2024 to USD 142.14 billion by 2030 at a CAGR of 4.06% in terms of value. The fertilizer sector covers the largest application for this market, led by the vital use of phosphoric acid as a crucial raw material in phosphate-based fertilizers that are used to boost agricultural productivity. This leadership is driven by increasing world food demand, increasing agricultural activity, and the requirement for greater crop output to fuel population growth. Phosphoric acid application in the production of fertilizers, as well as its uses in food processing, water treatment, and manufacturing in industries, has become vital for maintaining necessary industries, hence consolidating the sector's dominance in the industry.

The key players profiled in the report include OCP Group (Morocco), The Mosaic Company (US), PJSC PhosAgro (Russia), ICL Group Ltd (Israel), Nutrien Ltd. (Canada), EuroChem Group AG (Switzerland), Innophos (US), Solvay SA (Belgium), Ma’aden (Saudi Arabia), and IFFCO (India). These players have adopted various growth strategies to strengthen their position in the market. These include introducing new technologies, expansions, acquisitions, and product launches to acquire larger market shares.

To know about the assumptions considered for the study [**download the pdf brochure**](https://www.marketsandmarkets.com/pdfdownloadNew.asp?id=177852938)

OCP Group is one of the world's leading exporters of phosphate-based and other chemical products. The company is involved throughout the entire value chain, from mining and manufacturing to community development and education. It possesses over 70% of the world's phosphate reserves. The company operates three business segments: northern axis, central axis & phosboucraa, and head office and other activities. It supplies phosphoric acid through the northern axis and central axis & phosboucraa segment. OCP Group maintains a strong market presence across Europe, the Middle East & Africa, Asia Pacific, South America, and North America. In August 2022, OCP Group announced the expansion of its operations by launching a new plant to produce purified phosphoric acid. This plant will be managed by Euro Maroc Phosphore (EMAPHOS), a subsidiary of OCP Group, with an annual capacity of 280,000 tons starting from the fourth quarter of 2022.

PJSC PhosAgro is the leading producer of phosphate-based fertilizers. The company has a vertically integrated value chain from phosphate rock extraction to fertilizer manufacturing, with major production sites in Cherepovets, Balakovo, and Volkhoy. It operates through two segments: the phosphate segment and the nitrogen segment. Its production of phosphate fertilizers and phosphoric acid is managed under the phosphate business segment. The company mainly produces phosphoric acid for domestic use in manufacturing high-grade mineral fertilizers. In 2024, its phosphoric acid production reached 3.5 million tons, a 5.1% increase from the previous year due to upgrades at production units and better equipment utilization. PJSC PhosAgro focuses on the Russian market, leveraging its strong domestic distribution network and strengthening its position as Russia's leading low-cost producer of phosphate-based fertilizers.

The market for phosphoric acid is competitive, with five major companies controlling about 30-35% of the global market. OCP Group is the leading player in the sector, offering a wide range of phosphoric acid and having extensive integration into applications such as fertilizers, feed and food additives, detergents, and others. Mosaic Company has a strong market position centered on phosphoric acid and manages its global supply operations effectively. PJSC PhosAgro continues its growth trend by expanding through strategic acquisitions and market development. Regarding new-generation phosphoric acid, ICL Group Ltd and Nutrien Ltd. hold dominant market positions.

The remaining 65-70% of the market is made up of regional small-scale manufacturers. Market competition is driven by technological improvements in phosphoric acid and its increasing use in fertilizers, feed and food additives, detergents, water treatment chemicals, metal finishing, and various other industrial applications in developing economies.

# Top 10 Phosphoric Acid Producers in 2025 Dominate the Chemistry Game

### Published On : 04 Feb 2025

Phosphoric acid is a crucial chemical compound with applications spanning agriculture, food processing, and electronics. [Food-grade phosphoric acid](https://www.persistencemarketresearch.com/market-research/food-grade-phosphoric-acid-market.asp) is widely used in the food and beverage industry to enhance flavor and preserve shelf life in products such as soft drinks and processed foods. Meanwhile, [electronic-grade phosphoric acid](https://www.persistencemarketresearch.com/market-research/electronic-grade-phosphoric-acid-market.asp) plays a pivotal role in the tech sector, particularly in semiconductor manufacturing, microelectronics etching, and silicon wafer cleaning, where high purity is essential for precision and reliability.

Phosphoric acid producers are innovating to meet these needs with advanced production techniques and high-purity grades as industries demand more sustainable and specialized solutions. The compound's adaptability and functional benefits ensure its continued relevance in both traditional uses and emerging technologies.

## Explore the Leading 10 Producers of Phosphoric Acid in 2025

**1. OCP Group (Morocco)**

OCP Group dominates the phosphoric acid market, being the largest producer globally. The company's vertically integrated operations span mining, processing, and exporting phosphate products. OCP leverages Morocco's vast phosphate reserves, contributing significantly to the global fertilizer industry. Recent initiatives include investing in green hydrogen projects to enhance sustainable production and expanding its fertilizer complex in Africa to address regional agricultural needs.

**2. The Mosaic Company (USA)**

The Mosaic Company, headquartered in Florida, specializes in phosphates and potash, offering a comprehensive range of fertilizers. Mosaic integrates mining and manufacturing, ensuring efficient operations. Recent expansions include upgrading its phosphate facilities in Louisiana and adopting digital tools to optimize production processes. The company’s sustainability efforts include reducing carbon emissions and improving water management practices.

**3. PhosAgro (Russia)**

PhosAgro is renowned for producing high-purity phosphoric acid primarily used in fertilizers. Its products are favored for their low heavy metal content, supporting sustainable agricultural practices. PhosAgro's advancements in eco-friendly technologies and partnerships to promote biofertilizers underscore its leadership. The company continues to expand its export base, particularly in Europe and Asia.

**4. Yara International (Norway)**

Yara International is a major player in fertilizers and industrial solutions. Its phosphoric acid production supports its diverse product range, including crop nutrition and industrial applications. Yara focuses on sustainability through initiatives like producing fertilizers with lower carbon footprints. Recent developments include collaborations for green ammonia production and expanding its market reach in Africa and South America.

**5. IFFCO (India)**

IFFCO, India's leading fertilizer cooperative, is a significant phosphoric acid producer. The organization collaborates with global entities to secure raw materials and ensure consistent supply. IFFCO’s innovative approaches include producing nano fertilizers and adopting renewable energy in its operations. It has also strengthened its digital outreach to farmers, promoting efficient agricultural practices.

**6. ICL Group (Israel)**

ICL Group offers a diverse range of products, including phosphorus acid for industrial and agricultural applications. Recent sustainability initiatives and strategic acquisitions have strengthened its global presence, particularly in North America and Europe.

**7. EuroChem Group (Switzerland)**

EuroChem, with its diversified portfolio, includes significant phosphoric acid production capacity. The company invests in innovation, particularly in low-carbon technologies and nutrient efficiency solutions. Its vertically integrated model ensures a reliable supply chain for fertilizers. Recent activities involve establishing new plants and partnerships to strengthen its global distribution network.

**8. Nutrien (Canada)**

Nutrien is a key player in the phosphorus acid market, focusing on sustainable agricultural solutions. The company integrates phosphorus acid production into its fertilizer portfolio, supporting global food security. Nutrien's recent initiatives in digital agriculture and environmental stewardship highlight its commitment to innovation and sustainability.

**9. Sinofert Holdings (China)**

As one of China's largest chemical manufacturers, Sinofert Holdings plays a pivotal role in phosphorus acid production. Its robust distribution network supports China's growing agricultural sector. Recent upgrades to manufacturing facilities underscore its dedication to meeting domestic and international demand.

**10. Yuntianhua Group (China)**

Yuntianhua Group, a Chinese conglomerate, is a key phosphoric acid producer with extensive operations in fertilizers and chemicals. The company focuses on optimizing resource utilization and adhering to stringent environmental standards. Its efforts to modernize production facilities and expand its domestic and international footprint are noteworthy, addressing the growing demand for agricultural inputs.

## Leading Producers and Emerging Trends Drive the Phosphoric Acid Landscape in 2025

The phosphoric acid market in 2025 reflects a dynamic landscape shaped by technological advancements, sustainability initiatives, and expanding applications across industries. Leading producers are not only focused on scaling operations but also on adopting eco-friendly practices to align with global environmental goals.

With continued innovation and strategic investments, these companies are poised to meet the rising demand while promoting sustainable development. Their contributions underscore the critical role of phosphoric acid in addressing global challenges, particularly in food security and industrial development.

## Phosphoric acid

ICL is a leading producer of phosphoric acid for chemical manufacturing. We supply phosphoric acid as a raw material to customers producing downstream phosphate-based products such as phosphoric acid line cleaners, transition metal phosphate salts, metal phosphating solutions, and aluminum bright dip solutions.

[Explore Phosphoric acid](https://www.icl-phos-spec.com/about/p205-applications/chemical-manufacturing/)

## Polyphosphoric acid

ICL’s Polyphosphoric Acid (PPA) is supplied as raw material and recommended for use or evaluation in the following manufacturing processes: production of flame retardants phosphate esters, phosphorylation of polyols, production of phosphate ester surfactants, as a catalyst in organic reactions, and improving thermo-mechanical properties of asphalt cements.

[Explore Polyphosphoric acid](https://www.icl-phos-spec.com/about/p205-applications/chemical-manufacturing/)

## Bromine

ICL is the world’s largest producer of elemental bromine, supplying over 33% of the global demand. Bromine and bromine-based compounds are a fundamental component in a wide spectrum of industrial applications such as heat stabilizers, photographic emulsions, wood preservatives, catalyst (quaternary ammonium bromides), alkylation agents, special cleaning solvents, degreasing agents, and many more.

# Understanding the Production Process of Phosphoric Acid

Gabreilla Figueroa 30-Sep-2025

Phosphoric Acid is essential in fertilizers, food, pharmaceuticals, and metal treatment. Understanding its production enhances efficiency, sustainability, and regulatory compliance. With rising focus on green manufacturing, innovations in feedstock, energy use, and waste treatment are increasingly critical.

Phosphoric Acid is a vital inorganic chemical widely used across multiple industries, including fertilizers, food and beverages, pharmaceuticals, and metal treatment. It plays a crucial role in the production of phosphate-based fertilizers like **[DAP](https://www.chemanalyst.com/Pricing-data/diammonium-phosphate-dap-1179)** and MAP, serves as an acidity regulator in food products, and is also employed in rust-proofing treatments and detergents. Given its significance across both agricultural and industrial sectors, understanding the production process of Phosphoric Acid is essential for manufacturers, downstream users, and policymakers alike.

Comprehending the synthesis and processing steps of **[Phosphoric Acid](https://www.chemanalyst.com/Pricing-data/phosphoric-acid-1162)** helps stakeholders improve cost-efficiency, enhance sustainability, and ensure compliance with environmental standards. As global attention turns toward greener chemical manufacturing and resource optimization, innovations in feedstock selection, waste treatment, and energy use in Phosphoric Acid production are becoming increasingly important.

**Overview of the Production Process**

Phosphoric Acid is predominantly produced by two major methods: the wet process and the thermal process, with the former accounting for more than 90% of global production, especially for fertilizer-grade applications.

**1.           Wet Process:**

In this method, phosphate rock (primarily fluorapatite) is reacted with concentrated sulfuric acid to produce phosphoric acid and calcium sulphate (gypsum) as a by-product.

·                     The reaction is exothermic and conducted in large reactors under controlled temperature and agitation to optimize yield.

·                     Operating temperatures typically range from 70°C to 80°C.

·                     The crude phosphoric acid obtained (usually 26–30% P2O5 content) is then filtered and concentrated through evaporation systems to produce commercial-grade acid.

·                     Impurities such as fluorine, **[silica](https://www.chemanalyst.com/Pricing-data/silica-1304)**, and heavy metals are separated during this stage or treated downstream.

**2.           Thermal Process:**

Used primarily for food-grade and high-purity applications, this method involves burning elemental phosphorus in excess air to form phosphorus pentoxide (P2O5), which is then hydrated to yield phosphoric acid.

·                     Though more energy-intensive, this process results in higher purity and fewer impurities, making it suitable for pharmaceutical and food industries.

 ![](data:image/png;base64,)

**Raw Materials and Input Requirements**

The industrial production of Phosphoric Acid, particularly through the wet process, involves several critical inputs, primarily phosphate rock and **[sulfuric acid](https://www.chemanalyst.com/Pricing-data/sulphuric-acid-70)**. These raw materials are selected based on purity levels, mineral composition, and regional availability to ensure optimal process efficiency and product quality.

**?? Key Inputs Include:**

**•                    Phosphate Rock –** The principal raw material, typically containing calcium phosphate (fluorapatite). High-grade ores ensure better acid yield and lower impurities.

**•                    Sulfuric Acid (H2SO4) –** Reacts with phosphate rock to liberate phosphoric acid and generate gypsum (CaSO4) as a by-product.

**•                    Water –** Used in dilution, washing, and processing steps.

**•                    Utilities –** Include steam (for concentration), electricity (for material handling and controls), and process water.

•                    Flocculants/Clarifiers – Assist in separating solids (gypsum) from phosphoric acid slurry.

**Major Production Routes**

**1. Wet Process**

•             Most widely adopted industrial method (used for fertilizer-grade acid).

•             Phosphate rock reacts with sulfuric acid to produce phosphoric acid and gypsum.

•             Economical and scalable but requires filtration and concentration units.

•             Impurities such as fluorine and silica must be managed or removed.

**2. Thermal Process**

•             Produces ultra-pure food-grade or electronic-grade phosphoric acid.

•             Involves burning elemental phosphorus to form P2O5, then hydrating it to yield phosphoric acid.

•             High energy demand, but superior purity levels.

**?? Regional Trends:**

•    **China & India –** Leading producers via the wet process; focused on backward integration through domestic phosphate rock mining.

•             Morocco & North Africa – Home to vast phosphate reserves; global exporters of both raw material and phosphoric acid.

•     **USA & Europe** – Emphasis on high-purity and food-grade acid via thermal processes, with strong environmental controls.

**•             Equipment and Technology Used**

**•             Reaction Vessels –** For mixing phosphate rock with sulfuric acid.

• **Filter Systems** – Separate gypsum from the phosphoric acid slurry.

**•             Evaporators** – Used to concentrate crude acid to required P2O5 levels.

**•             Crystallizers** – Sometimes used to recover valuable by-products.

•           **Emission Control Units** – For fluorine, dust, and **[sulphur](https://www.chemanalyst.com/Pricing-data/sulphur-39)** compound recovery.

•       **SCADA/DCS Automation** – For process optimization, safety, and traceability.

**Environmental and Safety Considerations**

**Environmental Risks:**

•  **Fluoride Emissions –** Generated during acidulation; can harm vegetation and must be scrubbed.

•     **Gypsum Waste** – Requires proper disposal or repurposing (e.g., in construction).

•             **Heavy Metal Residues** – Vary based on rock source; must be managed via filtration or neutralization.

**Mitigation Strategies:**

**•             Closed-Loop Water Recycling** – Minimizes discharge.

•     **Stack Scrubbers** – Capture fluorine and sulphur emissions.

•         **Waste Management Protocols** – For safe gypsum stacking and leachate containment.

**Regulations:**

**•             EU (REACH) –** Requires registration and environmental risk management.

•     **US (EPA) –** Enforces air, water, and waste standards for phosphoric acid plants.

•    **India/China –** Strengthening environmental norms, especially around fluorine and solid waste.

**Conclusion and Future Innovations**

Phosphoric Acid is a strategic industrial chemical underpinning global food security, water treatment, and manufacturing. As environmental scrutiny intensifies, producers are investing in cleaner technologies, improved energy integration, and by-product valorisation.

**Emerging Trends:**

•     **Green Sulfuric Acid Production –** Reducing carbon intensity of upstream inputs.

•   **Phosphate Rock Beneficiation –** For higher-grade feedstock.

•          **AI-Driven Process Control –** Optimizing acid yield, energy use, and emissions.

•      **Circular Economy Approaches –** Recovering rare earths from phosphor gypsum and reusing waste streams.

With abundant applications and growing global demand, phosphoric acid production is evolving toward sustainable growth, digital efficiency, and resilient supply chains.

**FAQs**

**Q1. What is the primary method used to produce Phosphoric Acid?**

The most widely used method for producing Phosphoric Acid is the wet process. In this method, phosphate rock is reacted with sulfuric acid, producing phosphoric acid and gypsum (**[calcium sulphate](https://www.chemanalyst.com/Pricing-data/calcium-sulphate-1682)**) as a by-product. This process is commonly adopted in fertilizer production due to its cost-effectiveness and scalability. The wet process is typically carried out in large continuous reactors with filtration and concentration stages to obtain the desired acid strength and purity levels.

**Q2. What are the key environmental concerns in Phosphoric Acid production?**

**Environmental concerns associated with phosphoric acid manufacturing include:**

•             Fluoride and dust emissions released during phosphate rock acidulation.

•             Large volumes of phosphor gypsum waste requiring secure storage or disposal.

•             Heavy metals and other contaminants present in low-grade phosphate rock.

•             Effluent discharge containing residual acids and metals.

**To mitigate these issues, producers typically employ:**

•             Scrubber systems to capture fluoride emissions.

•             Gypsum stack management systems with leachate control.

•             Effluent treatment plants (ETPs) for water purification.

•             Compliance with global regulatory frameworks such as EU REACH, US EPA, and local environmental norms in major producing regions.

**Q3. Are there sustainable alternatives to conventional Phosphoric Acid production?**

**Yes, several sustainable advancements are being explored in phosphoric acid production:**

•             Recovery and reuse of phosphonyls, including extracting rare earth elements or using it in construction materials.

•             Cleaner beneficiation of phosphate rock to reduce impurities and improve process efficiency.

•             Co-production with waste heat recovery and energy integration to reduce emissions and operating costs.

•             Development of bio-based and circular phosphate sources, although still in early stages.

These innovations support the industry’s efforts to reduce environmental impact, conserve natural resources, and align with circular economy goals

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991)Abstract

This paper examines the need for innovation in phosphorus fertilizer production. An important area requiring action is the use of sulfuric acid in the wet chemical process (WCP), which is the dominant process in phosphate fertilizer production. About 50 % of the sulfuric acid produced worldwide is used for fertilizers, and ~95 % of the world's fertilizers are based on sulfuric acid. The latter is almost exclusively a by‐product of gas and oil production, so the production of conventional P fertilizer is largely dependent on the availability of oil and gas. In addition to rendering P fertilizer production independent of fossil raw materials, energy consumption, CO 2 emissions, phosphogypsum production and water consumption should also be considered. With the example of the PARFORCE process and the Improved Hard Process (IHP), new non‐sulfuric acid‐based alternatives are discussed with respect to overcoming the drawbacks of the classical WCP by being completely independent of fossil sources, working with renewable energies as the sole energy source, and the option of using seawater instead of fresh water. These new processes adhere to the principles of climate neutrality, zero waste production, low CO 2 footprint, water conservation, renewable energy use, and energy and resource efficiency. This demonstrates what sustainable innovation can look like from a production perspective. The discussion will focus on whether current incentives are sufficient to realize the sustainability innovations discussed.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991)Abstract

The article delves into the pressing necessity for innovation in the production of phosphorus fertilizers, with the aim of reducing dependency on fossil fuels, minimizing environmental impact, and enhancing sustainability through the implementation of alternative processes that utilize renewable energy and conserve resources.

**Keywords:**Phosphoric acid, Sustainability, Fertilizer, Resources, Phosphate rock

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991)Introduction

In September 2021, the world's population exceeded 8 billion. This came at a time when markets were already nervous about the situation in Eastern Europe, which was reflected in rising prices for phosphate (P) fertilizer. According to the United Nations, the world's population is expected to reach 9.8 billion by 2050, and this growth will inevitably lead to increased demand for food. It is evident that the provision of raw materials is essential for the sustenance of this expanding population. This is particularly true given the inability to feed the existing global population, let alone the projected growth in the future, without the application of industrial fertilizers. About half of today's crop yields can be directly attributed to the use of modern mineral fertilizers, mostly based on the elements phosphorus, nitrogen, and potassium.[[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0001), [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0002)]

In September 2015, just six years prior, the United Nations Sustainable Development Summit adopted the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, which comprises 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) at its core. Two SDG are particularly relevant here: SDG 2 is entitled “Zero hunger (achieve food security and improved nutrition and promote sustainable agriculture)”. SDG 12 is entitled “Responsible consumption and production (ensure sustainable consumption and production patterns)”. To meet SDG 12, the challenge to produce fertilizers under sustainability guidelines, the process from mining to processing must be carried out in a way that is as safe as possible for the environment, beneficial for the social structure of mining communities, regions, and countries, while aiming at optimizing resource efficiency. The key chemical intermediate in the production of P fertilizer is phosphoric acid (PA). As discussed below, the resource efficiency of PA production is far from optimal.

In this contribution we will first provide the necessary geological and socio‐economic background to the fertilizer element phosphorus. We then discuss the current low resource efficiency of P, and the environmental problems associated with the transition from phosphate rock (PR) to fertilizer. This is followed by suggestions for improvements in the mining and beneficiation stages and then, after presenting the current state of the art in PA production, alternative routes and considerations of whether it is possible to achieve a zero‐waste solution are discussed. This is in accordance with the process procedure that starts with PR to PA, which is then converted to P fertilizer. The paper concludes with an outlook and a future scenario.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991)The Socioeconomic and Geological Background of Phosphorus

In the case of raw materials, the general rule is that it is not the raw materials themselves that humanity needs, but the functions that they provide. If these functions can also be provided by other raw materials or other technical solutions, they are substitutable. We can distinguish between material substitution (material x against material y) or technological substitution, i. e., switching to an alternative technology that requires different raw materials.[[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0003), [4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0004)] There are three exceptions: the nutrient raw materials potassium, nitrogen, and phosphorus, which cannot be substituted, and which plants need as such.[[5]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0005) While there are practically unlimited resources of potassium in seawater and nitrogen in the atmosphere, the situation is different in the case of phosphorus. Although phosphorus is not a scarce or even a rare resource, it can be considered a limited planetary resource in terms of its availability for mining. Moreover, phosphorus has an inherent disadvantage as it is also a pollutant in many aquatic ecosystems. According to Steffen et al.,[[6]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0006) the biogeochemical fluxes of the nutrients nitrogen and phosphorus extend far beyond planetary boundaries, particularly through intensive agricultural zones, the impact of which also affects global nutrient flows. Although the P‐ore mineral apatite is ubiquitous and phosphorus is the 11 th most abundant element in the Earth's crust with an average concentration of ~1,120 mg kg−1, concentrations required to create a mineable deposit, which for P are predominantly sedimentary and igneous deposits, occur only in special geological situations. They are often unique to certain geological times and geographical locations, leading to country concentrations, which means that few countries mine P, similar to the situation with other commodities such as cobalt, lithium or platinum, which are currently essential for the energy transition. For sedimentary deposits, the largest high P deposits on Earth are found in the Permian Phosphoria formation (272–265 mill. years) of the western USA, in China in the Ediacaran (635–539 mill. years) and Cambrian (541–485 mill. years) belts,[[7]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0007) and in the North African phosphate belt formed in the Upper Cretaceous to Lower Tertiary (75–35 mill. years).[[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0008), [9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0009)] Russia, Brazil, and South Africa are major producers from magmatic deposits. 77 % of currently economically mineable phosphate deposits are concentrated in just four countries: China, Morocco, USA, and Russia.[[10]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0010)

Currently, a total of about 220 mill. t of marketable phosphate rock concentrate (PM) with a P 2 O 5 content of 67 mill. t is mined annually (about three quarters from sedimentary and one quarter from magmatic deposits).[[10]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0010) PM is processed into phosphorus fertilizer (83 %) or phosphorus chemicals (17 %), which are also used for food and feed.[[11]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0011) In the future, the use of phosphate in batteries for electric vehicles could become an increasing share. This is because sodium‐iron and lithium‐iron phosphate batteries are considered to be some of the most attractive electrode materials for e‐mobility.[[12]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0012)

We can distinguish two main types of producer countries: those with large domestic production but also large domestic consumption, such as China, which is both the world's largest producer and consumer, or the US. Then there are countries with large production volumes but limited domestic consumption and which can therefore be major exporters to the world market, such as Morocco. This country (including Western Sahara) is blessed with large, high‐grade deposits and, with 50 bill. t, has by far the largest PR reserves and also large resources.[[13]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0013) This makes it the second largest PR producer in the world after China and the world's largest exporter. It produced around 16.6 % of the world's PR in 2020,[[10]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0010) which covers around 35 % of raw phosphate exports, 49 % of the global phosphoric acid market share and exports around 4.5 % (9 mill. t) of global fertilizer.[[14]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0014) However, one also needs to consider exports of the final products monoammonium phosphate (MAP), diammonium phosphate (DAP) and triple superphosphate (TSP), which makes the supply situation more complex.[[15]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0015) While China is the largest producer of PR, it only exports intermediate or finished products. Globally, PR reserves are exceptionally high relative to production, much higher than for most other major commodities.[[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0005), [16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0016)] However, this ratio is only a momentary snapshot of a dynamic reserve/resource system and does not say anything about the lifetime. It can, however, serve as an early warning indicator[[5]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0005) and an indication of the time available to react and find solutions if a problem arises.[[17]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0017) In addition, the PR resources are more than 300 bill. T.[[10]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0010)

The regional concentration discussed above results in a relatively high Herfindahl‐Hirschman Index of HHI=2020, which is however not yet critical as it is below 5000. But supply is only one aspect. The other is the customer's desire to be supplied as cheaply and as safely as possible. The result is a desire for diversification of supply, which in turn counters the concentration of reserves. In fact, the US Geological Survey Mineral Commodity Summaries list 11 major reserve holders and producers in 1989, 12 in 1999, 15 in 2009 and 23 in 2023. In 2009, Saudi Arabia was listed in the USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries under ′Other Countries′. Meanwhile it has become the sixth largest PR producer in the world. In a supply risk assessment of the production of 53 commodities, the German Geological Survey (BGR) ranks phosphorus in 26 th place, which is practically a medium supply risk despite Morocco's strong market position.[[18]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0018)

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991)The Resource Efficiency of P

PA is the basis of almost all phosphorus chemicals, in particular of all P fertilizers. Its production starts with PR mining, and in order to understand the challenges met in PA production, it is necessary to describe the entire value chain from mine to product. It starts with the fact that the amount of PR which needs to be mined is strongly correlated with the resource efficiency of P, which is very low. It is between 5–10 % in terms of total nutrient use efficiency (TUE). TUE is the ratio between the amount of phosphorus in digested human food and the total amount of phosphorus in PR mined for human fertilizers and feed additives (run‐of‐mine ore grade). This low efficiency is due to losses of P at all stages of the supply chain.[[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0019), [20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0020), [21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0021), [22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0022), [23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0023), [24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0024)]

Losses of economically mineable phosphorus in mines and at the beneficiation stage,Low (multi‐year) nutrient use efficiency in crop production which is estimated to be 45–70 %,Losses of phosphorus in livestock production due to lack of recycling of phosphorus in animal carcasses, manure or food waste.[[25]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0025)

Recycling rates in industry are unknown, and recycling from wastewater depends on specific wastewater characteristics and legislation, which is in place in only a few countries.

With regard to losses in mining and beneficiation, a wide range of values from 40–80 % can be found in the literature, with a concentration of values between 60 and 72 %.[[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0026), [27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0027), [28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0028), [29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0029)] As approximately 75 %[[10]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0010) of the phosphates mined today are of sedimentary origin and the recovery rates in the beneficiation plants for sedimentary deposits are poor, this will be examined in detail. The International Fertilizer Development Center estimates that between 30 and 50 % of the P 2 O 5 equivalents in mined ore are not recovered and are contained in waste ponds.[[30]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0030) The reason for these low recovery efficiencies is the similar physical properties of the phosphate mineral francolite, Ca 5(PO 4,CO 3)3 F, the apatite variety typical of sedimentary P deposits, and the sterile gangue calcite, CaCO 3, which make them difficult to separate.[[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0031), [32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0032)] This situation is due to the high carbonate content of francolite. In the latter, up to 25 % of the phosphate lattice positions can be replaced by carbonate, making it a carbonate‐rich apatite.[[33]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0033) When phosphate is replaced by carbonate, the crystal surfaces of francolite tend to behave somewhat between apatite and calcite, making physical separation, e. g., by flotation, impossible, thus requiring chemical separation. This is in contrast to the case of magmatic deposits, where the barren fractions are usually silicates with significant differences in surface properties for flotation. In further processing of the concentrates hardly any interaction of the remaining silicates with acid takes place. In this case, apatite can be better separated by flotation, allowing producers to exploit ore grades as low as 4 % P 2 O 5. Lastly, it is necessary to look not only at single steps but to consider the total chain from the phosphate ore to the final production step for fertilizer and to achieve an overall best efficiency with minimum waste, i. e., environmental impact.[[34]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0034) In other words, one must also look at the waste generated by mining, beneficiation and subsequent processing. Phosphogypsum (PG), e. g., is a by‐product of PA production and has always been an environmental issue.

Looking critically at the whole chain, it must be noted that even in the third decade of the new millennium, the technology used for P recovery and processing dates back to the middle of the last century, when oil was abundant, and climate change was not an issue. For example, >80 % and almost exclusively from oil and gas using the Claus process. In the US, ~7 % originate from metal smelting.[[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0035), [36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0036)] This technology is highly vulnerable to geopolitical disruptions, economic imbalances, price fluctuations, uncertainties in oil and gas production, and much more. However, times have changed, and the world is facing new challenges. To meet the demands of the coming decades, modern processes must be based on the principles of

Climate neutralityZero waste productionLow CO 2 footprintWater savingRenewable energy useEnergy and resource efficiency.

We believe this is the standard by which sustainable production will be judged in the future, that this is the direction in which new developments must move, and why we have to leave trodden paths.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991)The Challenges of Phosphoric Acid Production

### The By‐Component Issues

The high content of harmful elements such as the transition metals cadmium and uranium in P ores will require additional purification measures in the short to medium term. Without these measures, the purity required by the European Fertilizer Regulation will not be achieved and the supply of P fertilizer will be jeopardized. Worse still, it is the heavy metal content of the fertilizer and not the phosphate content per se that is important. Therefore, an imposed limit, as in Europe, will have the effect of limiting the range of sources that P fertilizer suppliers can use. This measure may lead to a reduction of competition and the creation of oligopolistic market structures favoring producers of igneous PR. In the case of the EU, Russia is the largest trading partner for igneous PR. It is therefore essential to reduce these harmful elements at the earliest possible stage of PR processing. As a consequence, for sedimentary PR it is clear that additional chemical treatment steps are unavoidable if no alternative processing strategy is available. This is not problematic from a chemical engineering point of view, but the purification steps are costly, and this can have an impact on the price of the fertilizer. If changes or requirements in either the geological quality of the ore or regulatory requirements are not too abrupt, learning curves can contribute to overcome cost increases, which likewise can be offset by innovation, improvement and rationalization. An excellent example of such a learning curve in the natural resources sector is the innovation of the deteriorating quality of copper ores worldwide, with no increase in real prices since the end of the First World War.[[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0037), [38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0038)]

After further discussion of the environmental issues, we will look at the current state of technology and its environmental problems, before examining new processes that could pave the way for more environmentally friendly production of P fertilizers.

### The Environmental Issues

PA production relies on technology that originated in the 1960s. Although it has been improved over the decades, the underlying principle of sulfuric acid digestion has remained unchanged. One strategy to reduce processing costs in P fertilizer production is the co‐digestion of transition metal‐rich primary phosphate rock with less contaminated secondary phosphate sources, such as sewage sludge.[[39]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0039) The latter source is abundant globally and typically contains phosphate as iron or aluminum phosphate. While these compounds are readily digestible with sulfuric acid, the complex chemistry of trivalent metal sulfates makes this approach uneconomical.[[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0040), [41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0041)] This problem of transition metal contamination also applies to metals of anthropogenic origin. For example, copper (Cu) and zinc (Zn) are introduced by the weathering of metal roofs[[42]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0042) Cr and gutters, while the steel alloying elements chromium (Cr), nickel (Ni) or vanadium (V) are introduced by brake dust.[[43]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0043) Others, such as cadmium (Cd)[[44]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0044) or lead (Pb),[[45]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0045) have multiple sources that are not easily identified. The situation is exacerbated by fertilizer regulations against Cr as Cr (VI),[[46]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0046) which is highly toxic, although the vast majority is present as the less harmful Cr (III). This, in turn, results in costly and extensive cleaning efforts.

The production of PA is still energy intensive, particularly when sulfuric acid is used directly as a digestion agent without first burning sulfur. Since the latter is largely derived from crude oil processing and natural gas purification, the classic wet chemical process (WCP) is largely dependent on access to fossil feedstocks. Concisely, this means that PA production

Has, owed to calcination and sulfuric acid production, a carbon footprint that is unacceptable for modern chemical processes,Is highly vulnerable to economic changes in hydrocarbon markets, as seen in 2008 and more recently in the conflict with Russia, andIs highly dependent on the exploitation of fossil resources.

The most problematic issue, however, is PG, an unavoidable co‐product of PA production. Each ton of phosphoric acid produces 3.3–7.0 t of PG, which has no further technical use.[[47]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0047) In total, about 3.5 % of the phosphorus of the marketable phosphate rock ends in the PG waste, with 28 % ending up in coastal water, 58 % being stacked and only 14 % processed.[[48]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0048) Contamination with phosphate residues and transition metals, including radioactive actinides, necessitates landfilling. To illustrate the scale of this challenge, approximately 7 bill. t of PG were produced and stockpiled by 2016, with an additional 150–200 mill. t being added each year.[[48]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0048) Although PG could potentially serve as a resource for rare earth elements recovery and producing construction grade gypsum, there is currently no technical process operating on a large scale.[[48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0048), [49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0049), [50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0050)]

In fact, PA is just one example of how today's industrial chemical production is not prepared to meet the demands of the future with its challenges of a growing world population and limited resources.

The introduction of new technologies may be driven by future needs, but the technologies need to be more economically viable, too, in order to enter the markets. We are currently witnessing a complete realignment of the world's distribution of political, military and economic power. This represents not only an unprecedented challenge but also an opportunity. In the face of future challenges, the current turn of the tide may play the role of undertaker of the old and chaperon of the new.

This situation prompted us to look for alternative PA production processes that could better meet the demands of future chemical processing, particularly in terms of energy and resource efficiency, water consumption and environmental impact – in short, in accordance with the rules of sustainability. With secondary phosphate sources increasingly in focus in Europe, the question was whether hybrid processing of raw materials independent of their origin (i. e., either primary or secondary) was possible. Indeed, the origin‐independent processing of raw materials will become a key enabling success factor for a circular economy.[[51]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0051) To understand how and why we need to act, we will summarize the state of the art in PA production. Before doing so, however, we will take a brief look at the importance of sulfur, the preceding stages, mining and beneficiation.

### The Sulfur Issue

Sulfuric acid, which is mostly produced from sulfur, is currently an indispensable reagent with which the vast majority of PA is produced. Sulfuric acid is the cheapest acid and the most widely produced inorganic chemical in the developed world.[[52]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0052) For a long time, its market price has been stable between USD 60–80 per ton and is now rather volatile. In the first quarter of 2023, it was 157 USD/t, which is roughly double, but lower than in 2022, when it was as high as ~350 USD/t. In April 2024 it was 210 USD/t, in June 2024 it dropped down to 75 USD/t in Europe and 125 USD/t in the USA.[[53]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0053) The major sources of sulfur are oil and gas refineries, where H 2 S from oil refining (hydrotreater) and sour natural gas purification is converted to elemental sulfur in the Claus process. This source accounts for >75 % of global sulfur production. A smaller fraction of ~7 % is sulfur as a by‐product of copper, nickel, lead, molybdenum and zinc roasters and smelters[[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0036), [53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0053)] and an even smaller fraction via the Frasch process from natural sulfur deposits in salt deposits. However, in times when defossilization has become an issue, i. e., when fossil sources are to be abandoned as a measure to combat climate change, there will be less sulfur available from hydrocarbons. Recent geopolitical developments, such as the near‐total ban on Russian gas imports into the EU, have already significantly reduced the availability of sulfur from these sources. Despite this, the earth is sufficiently rich in sulfur, and in particular the sulfur contained in sulfide ores, which can again take the place of the hydrocarbon sulfur that it had before it was replaced by the cheaper hydrocarbon sulfur in the second half of the 20 th century.[[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0036), [54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0054)] Of course, sulfide roasting is an established process that has long been discussed as an alternative to sulfur combustion in the production of sulfuric acid.[[55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0055), [56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0056)] Sulfur is a unique commodity because, since the discovery of the giant Lacq sour gas field in southern France, which began production in 1958,[[57]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0057) the price of this commodity is no longer determined by efforts to extract the commodity from a reserve base that must be kept in balance with consumption through often substantial exploration efforts,[[4]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0004) but by efforts to find innovative uses for the ever‐growing supply of sulfur.[[54]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0054) The question of whether the current or expected mining of sulfide ores can be sufficient to compensate for the loss of sulfuric acid production from hydrocarbons can be answered by the fact that most of the sulfur generated by roasting base metal ore concentrates is already used in industrial processes. The shortfall that will occur as fossil fuels are phased out will most likely not be offset by increased base metal ore production.[[54]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0054)

Three sources of sulfur from sulfides can be used or reactivated: a) the sulfur from base metal sulfide ores and other sulfide ores, such as nickel or molybdenum, as mentioned above, which is always used for the production of sulfuric acid as an unavoidable by‐product (certainly by today's environmental standards it is unacceptable to simply release sulfur dioxide into the atmosphere with high chimneys, as was done in the past), b) the sulfur of pyrite as the major constituent of most base metal massive sulfide deposits, once regularly used in roasters to produce sulfuric acid, but since replaced by hydrocarbon sulfur, deposited in tailings dams, and c) the myriad of pyrite horizons and deposits as a by‐product of the exploration of base metal deposits using conventional electrical exploration methods. Sterile massive pyrite deposits, i. e., pyrite without base metals, cannot be distinguished from those with economic base metal values by these methods. The sulfides from the first two cases (a) and (b) are readily available, only the third case would require longer lead times.

The pyrite route, of course, has the disadvantage over the elemental sulfur route of having a coupled product, iron oxide. On the other hand, it is a step forward in terms of minimizing residues and waste, because pyrite, which – with a few exceptions – has to be produced anyway during the mining and beneficiation of base metal ores, can be used and does not have to be dumped and disposed of. This could be also a contribution to solve the worldwide acid mine drainage problem resulting from old and/ or not properly managed tailings dams.[[58]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0058) The byproduct iron oxide, which is too fine‐grained to be used as iron ore, can also be briquetted for use as iron ore. Cheap renewable energy can also be a game changer here. The amount of such iron ore as part of the total iron ore market is minimal and certainly without market influence. This iron ore solution could also solve the Paris Climate Agreement's requirement to be carbon‐free by 2050 (for Germany even more stringent by 2045), with the consequence that coke as a reduction medium has to be phased out and replaced by hydrogen. All steel companies in the developed world are working on solutions to achieve this goal.

A return to the sulfide route would of course mean that the sulfuric acid industry would have to be restructured. New roasting plants would have to be built in the centers of consumption. The same applies to the centers of the chemical industry, such as the former Duisburger Kupferhütte in Germany, which supplied the German chemical industry with sulfuric acid based on pyrite from Spain or Cyprus, e. g. Such a restructuring would not be gradual but could lead to temporary shortages and price increases. This is when the “feedback control loop of mineral supply” sets in.[[59]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0059) High prices are a great motivation for creative solutions and trigger reactions on the demand and supply side – always the old adage of the minerals industry: “The best cure for high prices is high prices”.[[55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0055), [56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0056)]

Another option for producing sulfuric acid is the Müller‐Kühne process, which uses anhydrite or gypsum. The latter two are available in almost unlimited quantities, but the process also works with coke and produces cement clinker as a by‐product.[[52]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0052)

In other words, the substitution of fossil sulfur with inorganic sulfur is at first sight a plausible exit strategy, but it is not yet foreseeable whether this option will be economically viable. While the growing base metals market, driven by the increasing demand for base metals, especially copper and nickel, for the energy transition, will always produce sulfuric acid as a by‐product for which uses have to be found, the alternative route to produce phosphoric acid would be to use other acids as will be discussed below. Again, renewable energy could be a game changer.

### The Fossil Resources Issue – or the Vulnerability Issue

Sulfur is a fossil resource, like oil, gas or coal, although it is not conceived of as such. The only difference is that, after use, it disappears in material flows which, according to current knowledge, are not climate effective. However, due to the origin of sulfur, it is apparent that any downstream process, be it sulfuric acid, be it phosphoric acid will be vulnerable to both economic changes and (geo)political crises. The price developments of sulfuric acid have been an unintended side‐effect of oil and gas ban with a particular impact on Europe.

Since sulfuric acid is currently not substitutable, PA production will be severely affected by sulfuric acid shortages or high prices. Any significant price increase will have an impact on food prices. With the world's population growing, this is a situation that calls for action, as opposed to adherence to established processes. This means that the food supply is also indirectly vulnerable to such developments.

As a next step, another unintended side‐effect can be P fertilizer production migrating to oil and gas producing countries, where oil is cheap. If, as in the case of Saudi Arabia, the country is also rich in PR, it is only logical that these producing countries will take advantage of this situation. One may complain about possibly different environmental standards there, but the continued use of fossil resources through the emission of CO 2 is tantamount to a continuing climate effect of P fertilizer production.

Last but not least, once P fertilizer production has migrated to PR producing countries, there will be a perpetual interest in keeping phosphate prices high to prevent customers from producing more at lower prices themselves. This is another unintended side‐effect that can affect P fertilizer prices for decades to come.

Briefly, as long as P fertilizer production depends on the wet chemical process with fossil resources at the beginning, the entire value chain is vulnerable to economic and (geo)political developments. All of this is accompanied by a number of unintended side‐effects with possible long‐term consequences.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991)Mining and Beneficiation

There are the classic mining and beneficiation methods, such as open pit or underground mining, and for beneficiation the methods, mostly used in combination of grinding, washing, scrubbing, and the use of hydrocyclones, calcination or flotation.[[60]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0060) At present, there is no radical new method for mining and processing on the horizon. This would have to be a leapfrog or disruptive innovation in phosphate mining and processing technology.[[61]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0061) For example, the gentlest mining method would be in‐situ leaching (ISL, solution mining), which only requires drilling. This method has been successfully applied to salt and has also been tried for copper. It even has become the most widely used method for uranium. In 2019, 57 % of uranium was produced by solution mining.[[62]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0062) However, this can cause serious groundwater problems.[[63]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0063) An option is the use of supercritical carbon dioxide (_sc_‐CO 2)/water for underground leaching of carbonate rock, such as PR.[[64]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0064) However, this method has not yet been applied to phosphate deposits. To the best knowledge of the authors, there is no application on the horizon for in‐situ leaching methods for phosphate.

Nonetheless, this does not preclude changes to improve resource efficiency and minimize environmental impacts. For example, selectivity could be increased to reduce mining losses.[[24]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0024) Underground methods can be highly selective. In addition, the use of tailings from processing as backfill reduces the need for surface tailings dams and minimizes surface impacts. There are excellent examples of barite, fluorite and tungsten mining in Germany and Austria with minimal environmental impacts.[[65]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0065) Selectivity can also be improved in open pit mining. More selective mining equipment than a dragline would be needed, such as bucket wheel excavators. If the waste is deposited further away with long belt systems, as is done in German lignite opencast mines,[[66]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0066) there would be enough space to work with low‐grade stockpiles, as is already done in some PR mines. PR can be processed at higher prices,[[67]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0067) or one tries to optimize resource efficiency by delaying mining stages. In anticipation of learning curves or higher price plateaus in the future, one could plan staged open pits with decreasing cut‐off grades over time, also using deeper seams that are below today's cut‐off grade.[[65]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0065)

It is well known that recovery at the beneficiation stage is negatively affected by rapid and large variations in the composition of the run‐of‐mine (ROM) ore entering the mill. It is possible to stabilize the composition of the ROM ore by using blending beds and feeding them with ore from different seams and locations in the deposit.[[68]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0068) There is an excellent example in lead‐zinc mining of a complex orebody with difficult intergrowth of the lead and zinc minerals and limits on the mercury content of the concentrates. The performance was optimized by a sophisticated sampling procedure guided by a sophisticated computer program.[[69]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0069) This requires close co‐operation between geologists, mining and milling engineers, a field now called geometallurgy.[[70](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0070), [71](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0071)] An example of how trace elements affect PR processing is iron in the wet chemical processing to PA, too high concentrations can severely hamper PA production. Conversely, a too low Fe 2 O 3 content has a negative effect on gypsum crystallization. The subsequent fertilizer production in turn benefits from trace amounts of Fe 2 O 3, which improves the granulation of the fertilizer and results in a low granular hardness of the final product.[[68]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0068)

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991)Phosphoric Acid Production

The production of PA, H 3 PO 4, from PR is typically carried out by wet chemical digestion with sulfuric acid (Figure [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-fig-0001)), while minor production quantities, such as via the Odda process sum up to ~10 %.[[72]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0072) Acid digestion, as the last process step before P fertilizer production can begin, must solve any problems that could not be solved during beneficiation, such as increasing the P grade, removing impurities, etc. It is the successful operation of this stage that determines whether the complete process from mining to phosphoric acid is economic.

Figure 1
[![Image 15: Figure 1](https://pmc-oa-opendata.s3.amazonaws.com/PMC11789991.1/CSSC-18-e202401155-g007.jpg)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/core/lw/2.0/html/tileshop_pmc/tileshop_pmc_inline.html?title=Click%20on%20image%20to%20zoom&p=PMC3&id=11789991_CSSC-18-e202401155-g007.jpg)

[Open in a new tab](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/figure/cssc202401155-fig-0001/)

The wet chemical process (WCP) for phosphoric acid production using the hemihydrate route. The gypsum (hemihydrate) initially formed is rich in phosphate and not marketable as such. It is therefore recrystallized in the presence of excess sulfuric acid to form marketable, almost phosphate‐free gypsum dihydrate, CaSO 4 ⋅ 2 H 2 O. Excess sulfuric acid, H 2 SO 4, from the recrystallisation step is recycled back into the digestion process, minimizing acid losses. It should be noted that only the hemihydrate route is suitable for producing marketable gypsum, but not all processes are operated in this way.

The by‐product, gypsum dihydrate (CaSO 4 ⋅ 2 H 2 O), called PG, results from the reaction of both, the calcium portion of the apatite and the remaining limestone fraction with the sulfate of the sulfuric acid. The digestion process to obtain phosphate‐free gypsum is subject to stringent process requirements. Only then can the gypsum be marketed. Otherwise, phosphate‐rich gypsum is obtained, which is expensive to dispose of. Handling and storage costs can be estimated at an approximate of 1.50 USD/t of PG produced, and lifetime storage cost at around 25 USD/t.[[73]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0073) The digestion process also leads to the mobilization of transition metals, which are removed from the crude PA in post‐treatment steps.[[52]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0052) The solubility of gypsum and metal salts in both water and PA must be considered when purifying the acid.

Crude PA is very impure and requires costly purification. When concentrated and left to stand, a significant proportion of the insoluble impurities settle as sludge, which is separated and disposed of. Depending on the application, the acid must be concentrated. For fertilizer production, H 3 PO 4 with 40–54 % P 2 O 5 is required, while for shipping the concentration is 52–72 % P 2 O 5. The evaporation process is technically complex, not only because of the highly corrosive nature of the acid and the precipitation of salts and gypsum, but also because of the release of acidic waste gases containing fluorine compounds and phosphoric acid mist. As PA is highly hygroscopic, the removal of water is very energy intensive. Much more extensive purification is possible by precipitation of the interfering ions followed by multi‐stage liquid‐liquid countercurrent extraction of H 3 PO 4.[[74](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0074), [75](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0075), [76](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0076), [77](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0077), [78](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0078), [79](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0079)]

Apart from the gypsum problem, sulfuric acid has another major disadvantage. In brief, this can be summarized as the unfavorable chemical properties of the sulfates formed during the digestion of P ores of primary or secondary origin containing trivalent ions, particularly Fe, Al, and rare earth elements. The resulting sulfates interact non‐specifically with various chemical entities over a fairly wide pH range between 3 and 11, forming slimes and precipitates that are extremely difficult, if not impossible, to remove. For this reason, any reasonable alternative to WCP must use an acid other than sulfuric acid.

These undesirable chemical interactions of trivalent metal cations also play a role in the classical WCP, but they are superimposed by the much more abundant divalent calcium and therefore appear less prominent. However, they contribute to the fact that crude PA, the so‐called “green acid”, must be purified at considerable expense. At present, pure PA is extracted from the crude PA obtained from the sulfuric acid digestion of PR. Alternative processes for extracting impurities from PA are not yet technically mature. However, it is possible to separate uranium from PA.[[78]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0078) It is this issue that makes “innocent” fertilizer production a political issue.

Not only can fertilizers serve as political and economic leverage, but the recovery and possible clandestine use of uranium is sometimes perceived as a cause for concern.[[80]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0080)

The problems associated with gypsum formation do not occur if nitric or hydrochloric acid is used instead of sulfuric acid. This can be done by analogy with the Odda process (Nitrophoska), the application of which is rather limited to Europe,[[81]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0081) where a P fertilizer is obtained by nitric acid digestion of fluorapatite.[[32]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0032) It should be noted, though, that one advantage of sulfuric acid is its lower price of 125 USD/t in the USA and 75 €/t in Europe[[53]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0053) compared to 35–37 % hydrochloric acid which is available at 168 USD/t in the US and 138 €/t in Europe.[[82]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0082) Nitric acid is even more expensive at 270 USD/t in the USA,[[83]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0083) not forgetting the high technical effort required to prevent the release of nitrous gases into the environment. Nonetheless, the use of nitric acid on an industrial scale is well mastered, as shown with the example of the Odda process where it is applied on a large scale. The main issue here is rather the market demand for calcium nitrate (Ca(NO 3)2), which is the co‐product of PA here.[[84]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0084) In fact, the market demand for both calcium nitrate and chloride (CaCl 2) is rather low on a global scale. Calcium nitrate is used as an ingredient in fertilizers, as a corrosion inhibitor in diesel fuel and in the manufacture of explosives and pyrotechnics. Calcium chloride is mainly used as a de‐icing agent.[[84]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0084) Therefore, if sulfuric acid is to be replaced by one of these acids, there must be a market for calcium nitrate or chloride. With the exception of de‐icing, CaCl 2 has no use and must be disposed of. Or the salt is converted to a market‐established product. Raw PA can be purified using established techniques.[[39]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0039)

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991)So Far so Good – can we do Better?

### Phosphate Recycling

Once used, the fate of phosphate is clear. Phosphorus is essential for human nutrition. Of the phosphorus mined, only 5–10 % of the phosphorus is digested and ends up in the wastewater.[[85](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0085), [86](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0086)] In wastewater treatment plants it is precipitated by the addition of iron, aluminum, or calcium salts, which bind the phosphate in insoluble form and in many cases make it inaccessible to agriculture. There have been attempts to reuse such sewage sludge, but this method suffers from the fact that the phosphate salts finely dispersed in the sludge are insoluble in water and not bioavailable.[[87]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0087) Instead, untreated sewage, where there had been no previous precipitation of phosphate salts, has been a traditional fertilizer in all parts of the world. In the US about half of the sewage sludge is made to fertilizer and about 8.6 mill. tons have been applied to American farm fields.[[88]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0088) But the application of sewage became more difficult because of concerns with respect to concentration and urbanization (with few huge sewage plants and high transportation costs). For treated sewage sludge it has been proposed to use microbially formed acids in the rhizobium of plants that can at least partially re‐solubilize phosphate,[[89]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0089) but this approach requires sophisticated agricultural technology to place the sludge directly into the rhizosphere of the plant.[[23]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0023) Another reason why direct fertilization with sewage sludge or sewage sludge ash (SSA) will not be feasible in most cases is the contamination of wastewater with transition metals, e. g., from traffic (brake dust). Other pollutants are pharmaceutical residues such as hormones from oral contraceptives or endocrine disrupting compounds (EDCs), i. e., hormone‐like substances such as plasticizers or perfluorinated organic acids (commonly known as PFAS, PFOA). Direct fertilization could introduce all these environmental pollutants into the food chain. Worse still, micro‐organisms that are resistant to antibiotics can be spread by the wind and cause antibiotic resistance throughout the local area, making pharmaceutical treatment of bacterial diseases difficult or even impossible.[[87]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0087)

The story is different when it comes to true P‐recycling. This is the production of PA from wastewater, sewage sludge or sewage sludge ash. This chemical, which is the universal P currency in both the chemical and fertilizer industries, is free of any pollutants, because it is produced in purities that meet the specifications of these industries.[[90]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0090)

Not only for these reasons, but also because there is a global market for recycled PA, P‐recycling is preferably done by recovering phosphoric acid from wastewater. However, the chemistry is complex and tedious, and there are very few processes on the market that can achieve this.[[91](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0091), [92](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0092)]

In addition to the recovery technologies, legal requirements are also necessary for P‐recycling to become established. Pioneers in this field include Switzerland, Germany and Austria, where corresponding laws already exist or are at least in preparation. In Germany, the Waste Sewage Sludge Ordinance (German AbfKlärV) regulates the recycling quotas for sewage sludge and sewage sludge ash. There are basically three different approaches to P‐recycling:

1. Processes at the sewage treatment plant:

– The P content of the sewage sludge must be reduced to below the threshold value in order to avoid an obligation under waste legislation.

– The majority of processes involve the formation of struvite, which is subject to a recycling obligation under the Closed Substance Cycle Waste Management Act, if applicable.

– Following the removal of pathogens, struvite is also approved as an EU fertilizer.

2. Processes from sewage sludge (in accordance with German AbfKlärV):

– The P‐content in the sewage sludge must be reduced to below the threshold value or below 50 % of the original value.

– The majority of processes involve the use of energy concepts with fertilizers that are not eligible for approval (carbonaceous residues).

3. The processing of SSA (in accordance with German AbfKlärV) is as follows:

– Direct use as fertilizer or as input material for the production of fertilizers (subject to the limitations of German fertilizer regulation).

– From 01. 01. 2029, only for ash from sewage sludge from plants with a capacity of ≤100,000 population equivalents (PE) that comply with the limit values for soil‐related utilization.

– From 01. 01. 2032 from plants with a capacity of ≤50,000 PE.

– EU fertilizers derived from ashes are subject to significant restrictions.

– Production of PA is costly but fulfils the obligation in a safe manner.

– 80 % isolated yield of the P content must be recovered.

In addition to sewage sludge, there are even more P sinks where phosphate vanishes. These are agricultural wastes and residues resulting from farming and harvesting activity, and also manure from livestock farming.

The dairy industry contributes as well as slaughterhouses the waste of which is typically bone material and in minor amount non‐bone material too. In coastal regions the latter is added waste from commercial fish processing. Another minor amount is household waste containing food material. A larger quantity, on the other hand, albeit in regionally varying proportions, results from biogas plants where the fermentation residues may contain up to 0.23 % P 2 O 5 but in a million tons scale.[[94]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0094)

To close the loop, a future‐proof process must be able to do both: PA production from both PR and secondary sources. The processes discussed below fulfil this requirement. Since the processing of the different feedstocks is not different, the technologies are not discussed in detail here and the reader is kindly referred to those sections.

### Circular Resources Chemistry as a Concept for the Future – Securing Raw Material Supply Through Holistic Approaches

Can concepts such as the chemistry of recyclables help to secure the raw material base for the future? Modern approaches to raw material extraction are less and less focused on individual target elements. Rather, they are holistic in nature and seek to maximize the use of raw materials once the ore has been extracted. However, there is still a strict separation between those industries that process primary raw materials and those that process secondary raw materials. In Europe, this has led to the development of parallel markets for the respective products, since in the vast majority of cases the reprocessed product does not reach the quality of the primary raw material. In fact, true recycling is rare, for example in the case of precious metals and copper. Most of the rest is downcycling, even when the secondary raw material is used to make a product with a defined composition, such as when scrap is used to make steel. In the latter case, however, the result is an alloy, not pure iron. Consequently, the concept of Circular Resources Chemistry (CRC) represents a complete turn away from the traditional way of working. The term describes the totality of processes and methods for the production of chemical raw materials, regardless of their origin. The concept removes the boundaries between primary raw materials (mining), secondary raw materials (recycling) and renewable raw materials (biomass). Holistic production techniques shift the boundaries of resource availability by not distinguishing between raw materials and residues (Figure [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-fig-0002)).
