Closed‐loop chemistry involves processes to produce chemical raw materials that are independent of their origin. There is no longer a distinction between raw materials and residues, and integrated production techniques shift the limits of resource availability.[[93]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0093)

The chemistry of recyclable materials is thus a consistent implementation of the closed‐loop recycling concept. It is the complex, holistic networking and interlocking of various production steps to form a central, individual process for each product (Figure [3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-fig-0003)). In contrast to earlier practice, in the chemistry of recyclable materials the function of a specific raw material is deliberately given priority.

Since it is irrelevant where the individual raw materials come from, waste products and residual materials from production processes or end‐of‐life products of a product, together with primary raw materials, become the starting material for another recovery process.[[51]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0051)

A characteristic feature is that recyclable materials that have already undergone one or more product cycles are regenerated to primary product quality, as the raw materials are extracted along a single technology chain. Only the entry points may differ, so that CRC implements the zero‐waste principle as far as possible. It should be borne in mind that zero waste is an ideal goal that cannot be fully achieved in commercial production, not to mention the limitations imposed by thermodynamics. However, minimizing the amount of waste as much as possible, as offered by this concept, comes remarkably close to this goal.[[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0051), [93](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0093)]

This is not just a theoretical consideration. The concept of circular resource chemistry has passed its baptism of fire. Several processes, including the COOL process (Li), the SSC process (rare earths), the RMF process (In, Ga, Sn) and the PARFORCE process (phosphate) have successfully made the leap from the laboratory bench to technical scale and are being operated commercially.[[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0039), [95](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0095), [96](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0096), [97](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0097), [98](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0098), [99](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0099), [100](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0100)]

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991)From Vulnerability Spaces to Technology Innovation Niches

The installation of additional sulfide ore roasting facilities for sulfuric acid production, which would require a new industry structure, remains uncertain.

One can argue that sulfide roasting is defeating the challenges of the future with methods from the past. However, this seemingly antique route opens a way to minimize waste production which cannot be avoided in the course of base metal mining and beneficiation to produce the metals needed for the energy transition. With new technologies using renewable energy for producing iron ore from oxidized pyrite with briquetting and hydrogen for reduction to iron and steel, this old process route could have a new lease of life.

In a free market economy, it is important to be technologically open in order to find the optimal, most economical technical solution under social, environmental, and governance aspect (SEG) constraints. The aim is to produce PA as a base for fertilizer via the most economic route. In this respect, it is worth mentioning here that the new processes described below do not use sulfuric acid. Therefore, they do not rely on sulfur from hydrocarbon sources, as is currently the case, or possibly from other sources such as sulfur from pyrite. Sulfur‐free PA production has the advantage of improving the resilience of the entire PA production system. Security of supply requires looking at the whole supply chain, not just the phosphate for the PA, but also the necessary materials upstream in the supply chain. New processes change the supply chain, and the more supply chains used, the more reliable the availability of the final product. Even if a new process is successful, it takes time to replace the old process, and in most cases, it is never fully replaced. So, there is a long period of increased resilience.

### Replacement

In view of the above‐said there is the need to get access to PA differently from using sulfuric acid. This requires entirely different processes with strict adherence to climate neutrality, high energy‐ and resource efficiency, zero waste production and low carbon emissions, not to forget water conservation and the use of renewable energy. The key to all this is replacement.

Replacement is the exchange of one process for another that is not dependent on a particular raw material whose availability or price is critical. The replacing process provides the product(s) with no difference in quality but uses different chemicals and auxiliaries. Replacement also encompasses the exchange of the energy source(s) required for a production process (Figure [4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-fig-0004)).

### The PARFORCE Process

One such technology to replace the established WCP is the PARFORCE process (Phosphoric Acid Recovery from Organic Residues and Chemicals by Electrochemistry). It was originally developed to overcome the problems of P‐recycling from SSA. It is a fully integrated zero waste process for which was shown that the process is robust enough to digest not only SSA but also PR or magnesium ammonium phosphate (MAP), MgNH 4 PO 4, also known as struvite. It is the avoidance of sulfuric acid that allows PARFORCE to be applied to a wide range of phosphate‐containing secondary raw materials such as production residues, calcium phosphates, bone meal ash and SSA. It produces market‐ready products without generating significant amounts of waste. In contrast to other PA production processes, the PARFORCE technology uses electrical energy only, and the generation of waste is kept to a minimum. As such it can be operated in an environmentally and climate‐friendly manner using renewable energy sources, such as the abundant solar energy available in Africa. Interestingly, the largest PR reserves are found in areas with good to excellent potential for the use of solar energy sources.[[101]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0101)

A very important issue is acid consumption. Traditionally, once a process becomes a wet chemical, excess acid is required to digest the ore (or secondary raw material) and complete the process within reasonable, i. e., economically viable, timescales. Typically, this excess acid has to be removed, i. e., the spent chemical is not only lost, but is actually over‐consumed by the alkalis required to adjust the pH to neutrality. This is not only questionable in terms of resource efficiency, but also typically the economic death knell. In the WCP for PA production, this problem has been solved by reintegrating excess acid into the digestion reactor when sulfuric acid is used as the digestion medium (Figure [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-fig-0001)).

In the case of hydrochloric acid, the situation becomes even more favorable and economically interesting if solar energy is available. In this case, the intermediate product CaCl 2, which is an almost useless, hardly marketable compound,[[84]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0084) can be split electrochemically. One product is Ca(OH)2 (slaked lime), for which there is a global market. The other product is HCl, which is recycled back into the digester so that no excess acid is lost. The only acid consumed is the hydrochloric acid required for the digestion step in stoichiometric quantities according to the ore composition.

Another key feature is that no fresh water is required. Sea water can be used instead. Since the digestion process is performed with hydrochloric acid, HCl, there is no reason not to use seawater. The sodium chloride, NaCl, contained therein (c≈35 g/L) is separated by bipolar electrodialysis. The products, HCl and NaOH, are the same as those obtained in the regeneration cycle (Figure [5b](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-fig-0005)), where NaCl is split to produce slaked lime from the CaCl 2. The co‐product HCl is used to reduce the amount of fresh HCl. No water is lost during the entire process. This makes it suitable for use in arid, sunny regions (Figure [5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-fig-0005)).

### The Improved Hard Process (IHP)

Another process bridging the gap to future PR processing is the Improved Hard Process from NovaPhos Inc. In Australia, Avenira operates a IHP plant for the production of PA.[[102]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0102) In contrast to both WCP and PARFORCE this is a thermal process, which however has little in common with the classical production of thermal phosphoric acid (Figure [6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-fig-0006)).[[52]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0052)

By keeping the process short, mostly by eliminating expensive beneficiation steps such as flotation, the overall process is more cost effective and less energy intensive. However, the primary product is phosphorus oxide, P 4 O 10, what is a clear distinction from the white phosphorus, P 4, generated in the thermal process.

The improved hard process (NovaPhos). The main advantage is that it tolerates low‐grade PR that does not require further treatment. Calcination is essential to remove interfering impurities such as Al and Fe but is energy intensive and uses petroleum coke. After wet chemical digestion, PA is obtained.[[103](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0103), [104](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0104), [105](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0105)]

The IHP has several advantages: (i) there is no elemental P 4 to be condensed, (ii) there is no combustion of P 4 to P 4 O 10 with all its drawbacks regarding corrosion, flue gas cleaning, etc., (iii) the process is much shorter and simpler, and (iv) there is no waste. Instead, the calcium silicate obtained can be used to make cement. By using coke made from biomass, the use of the silicate residue in the cement industry can help reduce the CO 2 footprint of the latter. In addition, the calcium silicate quality obtained can also be used in soil amendment, as it is chemically inert and does not leach toxins or degrade over time. It has a porous structure that can also absorb water from saturated soils and release the moisture as the soil dries.

The option of using the silicate residue in cement industry renders the IHP suitable for low concentration PR with 10–15 % P 2 O 5. In particular, for the same reason, the iron, aluminum and magnesium contents can be much higher than for WCP and PARFORCE.

The IHP is designed to produce only products and by‐products for which there is a market. The thermal strategy avoids the need to digest the PR with sulfuric acid, so the IHP does not produce PG, which must be disposed of. Yet, volatile heavy metal compounds can pass through the venturi scrubber and eventually become an impurity of the PA.

It is within the logic of the process design that the fluoride content of the PR is not a problem. It can be assumed that during the thermal treatment the fluoride is fixed as calcium fluoride, CaF 2. As there is no acid treatment, no release to the environment is to be expected. However, there is no information on the quality and composition of the flue gas or how the fluoride content is treated.

Comparing these new, alternative processes with the classical WCP, it becomes clear that the differences lie in a much better energy consumption as well as in a mostly complete valorization of all products, i. e., also of the by‐products. In both cases, no PG is generated, so there is no environmental problem. Both approaches aim at avoiding net CO 2 emissions into the atmosphere. ## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991)What About the Rest? Or: Zero Waste is More than Just a Goal

We have shown above that there are ways to minimize waste in the value‐added stages after the mining stage to produce P fertilizer, or even to produce it without waste. The mining stage will be discussed again.

### Circularity and Sustainability: Renewable Energy as a Game Changer

The old approach (“Old”) and the new approach (“New”) under discussion follow fundamentally different technologies to produce PA (Figure [8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-fig-0008)). The Old is a one‐way, waste‐intensive design. Here, PA is produced using sulfuric acid from sulfur, which is mainly produced from hydrocarbons using the Claus process. Although the production of sulfuric acid is exothermic, the entire process chain from the fossil raw materials oil and gas to PA consumes considerable amounts of energy. One ton of PA produces about five tons of PG.[[47]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0047) Despite considerable efforts and the search for economic uses in recent decades, only 14 % of PG can be used economically.[[48]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0048) Approximately 10 % is dumped into the ocean, a practice that is being phased out.[[106]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0106) The vast majority is disposed of in PG landfills, some of which contain heavy metals and long‐lived radioactive elements.[[48]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0048) In contrast, the new technologies exemplify zero waste circular economy production design. Instead of sulfuric acid, other acids, such as hydrochloric acid (HCl), are used to digest PR. Of course, the production of hydrochloric acid also requires energy, but it is also a chlorine sink because the chlorine obtained from the chloralkali process is used to produce vinyl chloride monomer and HCl.[[107]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0107) If there is also a market for the by‐products and co‐products, the new types of PA production are waste‐free.

It should be noted, however, that the scope and objectives of the new and old approaches are not the same in terms of life cycle analysis.[[108]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0108) For example, nitric acid‐based processes (also of the old type) give access only to nitrate‐containing NPK fertilizers, not to all P fertilizers. However, only 10 % of current production uses nitric acid, such as the Odda process.[[72]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0072) There are also differences in the purity of the PA produced. Last but not least, one must not forget that nitric acid is produced from ammonia, which is responsible for 1 % of annual CO 2 emissions. The new ones seem to be superior.[[106]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0106) As this, however, requires a differentiated quantitative analysis, which is beyond the scope of this paper, only a qualitative discussion is given here.

As shown in Table [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-tbl-0001), the energy consumption of the two process types differ significantly. A large part of the energy for the WCP is required for calcination and to produce sulfur. As pointed out above, elemental sulfur is mainly produced as a by‐product of petroleum refining and natural gas processing. This has replaced much of the sulfur previously produced by the very energy‐intensive Frasch process, which produces sulfur from elemental sulfur deposits in salt domes or by roasting pyrite. These processes account for only a small portion of today's sulfur production. In the energy balance, the energy required for sulfur, sulfuric acid and the end product PA is only partially offset by the exothermic process of sulfur oxidation. This concept is only valid if all sulfur oxidation, sulfuric acid production, and PA processing are performed at one site to allow for heat management and process heat transport. This is represented by the gray portion of the energy symbol in Figure [8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-fig-0008), upper left. Therefore, from an energy efficiency perspective, it is advantageous to produce PA where the oil refinery produces sulfur as a by‐product. This has been the case in Saudi Arabia for more than a decade.[[109]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0109)

On the other side, the production of hydrochloric and nitric acid, respectively, requires considerable energy too. The advantage of the volatile mineral acids such as HCl is its recyclability, i. e., the process does not consume much more than the stoichiometrically required amount of acid. It has to be pointed out, though, that both WCP and PARFORCE recirculate excess acid, what in turn means that only the digestive loss needs to be replenished. IHP, on the other hand, is a thermal process that does not use acid digestion. The qualitative comparison suggests that if renewable energy, including biomass, were to be used instead of fossil fuels, the new processes were significantly more effective and sustainable in an overall assessment,[[106]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0106) although only a qualitative discussion is given here.

Against this background, it seems obvious that the energy transition to renewable energy is a game changer in PA production. A full quantitative assessment of existing approaches is the subject of ongoing studies and is beyond the scope of this paper, which aims to highlight where and why rethinking established processes can provide solutions.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991)General Considerations

Let us begin with a fundamental discussion. The cultural and technological development of mankind has only been possible through the use of mineral resources. Therefore, our technological development has been labelled according to raw materials: Stone Age, Bronze Age, Iron Age and now what many call the Silicon Age. Feeding a growing population has only become possible through the use of mineral fertilizers made up of the elements phosphorus, potassium and nitrogen. The period since the importance of mineral fertilizers was first recognized – Justus von Liebig's publication on agricultural chemistry in 1840 – could therefore also be called the mineral fertilizer age. Nitrogen can be produced by the Haber‐Bosch process from the unlimited supply of nitrogen in the air, and potassium can theoretically be produced from the unlimited supply of potassium in seawater. On a technical scale, for economic reasons this is done only from potash seams and salt domes by underground mining. Primary phosphorus must be extracted exclusively from sedimentary or magmatic deposits by mining as described above.

It has been argued that mankind has extracted so many raw materials from the geosphere and transferred them to the technosphere during the industrial era – since atoms do not disappear – that mankind could only live on secondary raw materials. However, this is a fallacy even for metals with high recycling rates, for several reasons that will not be discussed in detail here. One fundamental reason is that 100 % recycling is thermodynamically impossible. Another issue, which is even more relevant, is the ever‐increasing world population. For phosphorus, the use of secondary phosphate is still in its infancy in some areas of Europe and a few other countries. However, even with improved phosphorus resource efficiency through better precision farming, better plant mycorrhizal systems to take up hard‐to‐access phosphate in the soil, or other as yet unknown disruptive (leap) innovations,[[61]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0061) there will always be losses. For example, there is no way to completely prevent fertilizer from being washed away by rain in open fields and transported to the sea in run‐off water. In addition, with a growing world population, the demand for phosphate is still growing and will continue to grow for the foreseeable future. We must therefore recognize that some exploitation of primary phosphate deposits will always be necessary.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991)New or Improved Solutions

If our energy system changes drastically with the transition to renewable energies, a new solution for sedimentary P‐ore could also be envisaged. This is where the electrochemical approach could be helpful. As mentioned above, francolite is a major problem in PR beneficiation. However, if renewable energy is used, carbonate‐rich impurities may be much better tolerated because excess calcium is converted to marketable slaked lime, Ca(OH)2. In other words, if less francolite ends up in the tailings, P efficiency is increased, beneficiation costs are reduced, and the additional process cost is economically offset by the slaked lime sales revenue. As an alternative, calcium is converted thermally to the Ca‐silicate which is then used in cement production for instance. This is the reason why both PARFORCE and IHP can cope with lower PR qualities.

There is a slightly different solution for igneous phosphate rock. In Russia, the problem is solved by valorizing the nepheline tailings in igneous phosphate mining. Despite integrated process control, large quantities of residue are produced and the potential of nepheline, [Na 0.75 K 0.25]AlSiO 4, as a source of aluminum was recognized early on. For 1 ton of Al 2 O 3, ~4 t of nepheline concentrate and ~12 t of limestone, CaCO 3, are required. The by‐products are ~7.5 t nepheline slurry, ~10 t Portland cement and ~1 t soda, Na 2 CO 3. Reaction of the nepheline slurry with this soda produces pirssonite, Na 2 Ca(CO 3)2 ⋅ 2H 2 O, which can be used directly as a replacement for limestone. Further processing of the residue for silica hydrogel provides saleable silica gel while regenerating the soda, which is reused after concentration. Activities are currently focused on the only significant residue, dicalcium silicate, Ca 2 SiO 4, which is known as belite and is a key component of cement. When these efforts are completed, approximately 90 % of the ~6.5 mill. t/a tailings will be marketed as products, converting ~8 mill. USD in landfill costs per year into revenues that could exceed that amount. This represents not only a remarkable contribution to resource efficiency, but also processes that allow further exploitation of deposits whose viability has become an issue, without the need for new mines and environmental disturbance elsewhere.[[115]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0115)

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991)Concluding Remarks and Discussion

The considerations outlined lead to a thought experiment: In our market economy, mining is a business like any other with investors seeking to maximize their return on investment (ROI).[[116]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0116) However, mining is inherently risky activity due to the geological uncertainties in estimating the ore input, leading to higher overall business risk and, consequently, the expectation of a higher rate of return.[[117]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0117) To achieve the optimum ROI, the cut‐off grade of the ore must be optimized.[[118](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0118), [119](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0119)] Overburden from mining is usually a “by‐product” for which later uses are sought to minimize the cost of disposal, but these are usually only cost aspects at the planning stage, not revenue aspects. In the context of planetary health and sustainable development, an entirely different approach could be envisaged – one that aims not to optimize ROI but to maximize the value of the usable material extracted from the geosphere. This would involve designing an operation that maximizes the proportion of the total rock to be moved that can be used in economic activities and minimizes the proportion that has to be dumped. In this scenario, mining would become a subsidiary service industry, simply providing the necessary raw materials for the subsequent value‐adding industrial stages.

While the international implementation of such systems is complex due to the global nature of raw material markets, two critical aspects warrant discussion. However, if the system's optimization relies on government involvement in securing raw material supplies, it could signal a shift toward a planned economy. Historical comparisons suggest that free‐market economies with robust government regulation offer the best environmental protection. Taxpayers’ money should be allocated not for industry's core task, but for the SDGs, such as education or public health.

What do we do with the remaining impurities, such as the transition metals? This is not an easy question to answer, but once these metals are no longer trapped in a phosphogypsum matrix, from which they can hardly be released under economic conditions,[[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0047), [120](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0120)] it is possible to think about using them on an industrial scale. Cadmium, for example, is generally regarded as an environmental pollutant. But it is also essential for the production of thin‐film solar cells. By shedding new light on an old problem, a pollutant becomes an enabler for renewable energy production. Lanthanides, better known as rare earth elements, are essential for the manufacture of wind turbines. The real leftovers are the radioactive actinides. Whether these will be disposed of, preferably under state control, or whether certain metals will be put to good use, for example in nuclear medicine, is not yet clear. It is clear, however, that this future prospect of PA production is a key enabler for future technologies rather than a cause of problems such as those associated with last century's technology.

The alternative PA production processes presented here exemplify how existing challenges can be overcome through the deliberate use of new technologies. Solar energy replaces fossil fuels in the production of PA, and hydrochloric acid (HCl) replaces sulfuric acid. HCl, a by‐product of the production of caustic soda from sodium chloride, also aids in reducing chlorine compounds in the chemical industry, aligning with European Commission policies.[[121]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-bib-0121) This issue appears in a new light in the context of efforts to defossilize industrial chemical production, particularly the production of P fertilizers.

The release of carbon dioxide (CO 2) into the atmosphere, though unavoidable by any process, is reduced to an unavoidable minimum. This unavoidable amount is due solely to the acid digestion of PR, during which the carbonate fraction of the phosphate ore, i. e., calcium carbonate, CaCO 3, and francolite, Ca 5(PO 4,CO 3)3 F, decompose and release CO 2 irrespective of the process applied. This is because both wet chemical acid treatment and thermal treatment cause these minerals to decompose, liberating CO 2.

This geological CO 2 comes exclusively from the ore, not from energy production, and is therefore an unavoidable by‐product of P fertilizer production that must be accepted. If the total CO 2 release is understood as the sum of anthropogenic and natural CO 2 release, only the latter is effective (Figure [9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11789991#cssc202401155-fig-0009)).

A novel approach to PR mining and processing to P.

In summary, these novel approaches result in

(1) A new mining system that operates with lower losses, lower grade stockpiles and/or delayed mining phases with lower cut‐off grades.

(2) Full utilization of the entire resource content as marketable units, including

a. Phosphoric acid, H 3 PO 4

b. Slaked lime, Ca(OH)2

c. Rare earth elements

d. Calcium silicate.

(3) Safe and controlled use or disposal of actinides.

(4) Avoidance of phosphogypsum dumps.

(5) Substitution of fossil raw materials by solar energy.

(6) Use of seawater instead of fresh water.

(7) Reduced carbon footprint.

Ultimately, this approach aligns closely with the goals of zero waste production processes. As a commercial process, it also shows that chemical processes that contribute to achieving climate goals can be run economically, even on a large scale.

# 16 Phosphoric Acid Manufacturers in 2026

This section provides an overview for phosphoric acid as well as their applications and principles. Also, please take a look at
[the list of 16 phosphoric acid manufacturers](#manufacturers) and [their company rankings](#rankings). Here are the top-ranked phosphoric acid companies as of August, 2026: 1.Innophos Inc., 2.CamaChem, 3.VALCO GROUP.

Table of Contents

## What Is Phosphoric Acid?

Phosphoric acid, alongside nitrogen and [potassium](https://us.metoree.com/categories/6882), is one of the three primary elements of fertilizer and an oxoacid of phosphorus.

Also known as orthophosphoric acid, it promotes flowering and fruiting in plants and is a crucial component of DNA and RNA, the genetic material, and cell membranes in living organisms. Phosphoric acid is essential for life.

As a natural resource, phosphorus is found as phosphate ore, and its depletion is concerning. Phosphoric acid is industrially produced through two methods: dry and wet.

### Uses of Phosphoric Acid

Phosphoric acid is widely used in industry as a raw material for various phosphates, chemical polishing agents for aluminum, rust inhibitors for metals, metal cleaning agents, can cleaners, refractory auxiliaries, paint preparation agents, activated sludge processes, [phosphate fertilizers](https://us.metoree.com/categories/7683), and reagents.

In food applications, it serves as an acidifier for beverages, a pH adjuster in brewing, and a raw material for phosphoric acid additives in juices, colas, and other food products.

It is also utilized as a raw material for dyeing auxiliaries, petrochemical catalysts, and pharmaceutical additives.

### Properties of Phosphoric Acid

Phosphoric acid has a melting point of 42.35°C and a boiling point of 407°C. When melted, it appears as a clear, colorless liquid.

It is soluble in water, alcohol, and ether. Liquid anhydrous phosphoric acid is a strong acid and a high conductor of electricity.

### Structure of Phosphoric Acid

![Figure 1. Structure of phosphoric acid](https://metoree.com/wpdrs/wp-content/uploads/2023/01/6558_Phosphoric-Acid_リン酸-1.png)

![Figure 1. Structure of phosphoric acid](https://metoree.com/wpdrs/wp-content/uploads/2023/01/6558_Phosphoric-Acid_リン酸-1.png)

**Figure 1. Structure of Phosphoric Acid**

The chemical formula of phosphoric acid is H3PO4. Its molar mass is 98.00 g/mol, and its density at 25°C is 1.892. Pure phosphoric acid forms unstable crystals of the orthorhombic system.

Phosphoric acid ions adopt a tetrahedral structure. The bond distance between phosphorus and oxygen (P-O) in aluminum phosphoric acid crystals is 152 pm.

### Other Information on Phosphoric Acid

#### 1. Synthesis of Phosphoric Acid

Burning phosphorus produces diphosphorus pentoxide, which, when dissolved in a dilute aqueous solution of phosphoric acid, yields pure phosphoric acid. This thermal synthesis method is environmentally friendly, although impurities in the mined phosphorus must be removed.

Phosphoric acid can also be obtained by reacting approximately 35% [sulfuric acid](https://us.metoree.com/categories/6704) with phosphate ore. This wet synthesis method can be purified through filtration, but may contain impurities such as hydrofluoric acid, resulting in lower purity than the thermal synthesis method.

#### 2. Structure of Phosphoric Acid Ion

![Figure 2. Structure of phosphate ion](https://metoree.com/wpdrs/wp-content/uploads/2023/01/6558_Phosphoric-Acid_リン酸-2.png)

![Figure 2. Structure of phosphate ion](https://metoree.com/wpdrs/wp-content/uploads/2023/01/6558_Phosphoric-Acid_リン酸-2.png)

**Figure 2. Structure of Phosphoric Acid Ion**

Phosphoric acid, a trivalent acid, ionizes in aqueous solution, releasing three hydrogen ions. The ionization stages produce dihydrogen phosphate (H2PO4-), hydrogen phosphate (HPO42-), and phosphate (PO43-) ions.

The pKa values at 25°C are pKa1 = 2.12, pKa2 = 7.21, and pKa3 = 12.67, respectively.

#### 3. Dehydration Reaction of Phosphoric Acid

![Figure 3. Structure of condensed phosphoric acid](https://metoree.com/wpdrs/wp-content/uploads/2023/01/6558_Phosphoric-Acid_リン酸-3.png)

![Figure 3. Structure of condensed phosphoric acid](https://metoree.com/wpdrs/wp-content/uploads/2023/01/6558_Phosphoric-Acid_リン酸-3.png)

**Figure 3. Structure of Condensed Phosphoric Acid**

Upon heating, phosphoric acid undergoes a dehydration reaction. At 150°C, it becomes anhydrous, and at 200°C, two molecules react to form pyrophosphoric acid. Higher temperatures lead to the formation of meta-phosphoric acid, a condensed compound, when one water molecule per phosphoric acid unit is desorbed. Diphosphorus pentoxide, produced by further dehydration, reacts violently with water and is used as a drying agent.

#### 4. Phosphoric Acid and Health

Phosphorus, found in foods of biological origin such as vegetables and meat, is used as an acidity additive in foods and beverages. It is a necessary mineral for the human body, with recommended daily amounts set by health authorities.

In 1950, the company started the production of phosphate fertilizer at the Koriyama factory and the production of insecticides at the Miharu factory. In 1970, it began producing phosphoric acid, and in 1971, it started making chromium compounds.

#### Manufacturer Overview

Kanto Chemical Co. Inc., founded in 1944 and headquartered in Tokyo, Japan, is a reagent manufacturer with overseas affiliates in other countries, including China, France, USA, Taiwan, and Malaysia.

The name "orthophosphoric acid" can be used to distinguish this specific acid from other "phosphoric acids", such as pyrophosphoric acid. Nevertheless, the term "phosphoric acid" often means this specific compound; and that is the current IUPAC nomenclature.

## Production

[edit]

Phosphoric acid is produced industrially by one of two routes, wet processes and dry.

### Wet process

[edit]

In the wet process, phosphate-containing minerals such as calcium hydroxyapatite or fluorapatite are treated with sulfuric acid.

:   Ca5(PO4)3OH + 5 H2SO4 → 3 H3PO4 + 5 CaSO4 + H2O
:   Ca5(PO4)3F + 5 H2SO4 → 3 H3PO4 + 5 CaSO4 + HF [...] ### Dry process

[edit]

To produce food-grade phosphoric acid, phosphate ore is first reduced with coke "Coke (fuel)") in an electric arc furnace, to give elemental phosphorus. This process is also known as the thermal process or the electric furnace process. Silica is also added, resulting in the production of calcium silicate slag. Elemental phosphorus is distilled out of the furnace and burned with air to produce high-purity phosphorus pentoxide, which is dissolved in water to make phosphoric acid. The thermal process produces phosphoric acid with a very high concentration of P2O5 (about 85%) and a low level of impurities. [...] Phosphoric acid produced from phosphate rock or thermal processes often requires purification. A common purification method is liquid–liquid extraction, which involves the separation of phosphoric acid from water and other impurities using organic solvents, such as tributyl phosphate (TBP), methyl isobutyl ketone (MIBK), or n-octanol. Nanofiltration involves the use of a premodified nanofiltration membrane, which is functionalized by a deposit of a high molecular weight polycationic polymer of polyethyleneimines. Nanofiltration has been shown to significantly reduce the concentrations of various impurities, including cadmium, aluminum, iron, and rare earth elements. The laboratory and industrial pilot scale results showed that this process allows the production of food-grade phosphoric

Chemical compound

**Phosphoric acid** (orthophosphoric acid, monophosphoric acid or phosphoric(V) acid) is a colorless, odorless [phosphorus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphorus "Phosphorus")-containing [solid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid "Solid"), and [inorganic compound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inorganic_compound "Inorganic compound") with the [chemical formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_formula "Chemical formula") [H](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen "Hydrogen")3[P](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphorus "Phosphorus")[O](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen "Oxygen")4. It is commonly encountered as an 85% [aqueous solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aqueous_solution "Aqueous solution"), which is a colourless, odourless, and non-[volatile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volatility_(chemistry) "Volatility (chemistry)") syrupy liquid. It is a major industrial chemical, being a component of many fertilizers.

The compound is an [acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acid "Acid"). Removal of all three H+ ions gives the [phosphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphate "Phosphate") ion PO3−4. Removal of one or two protons gives [dihydrogen phosphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphate "Phosphate") ion H2PO−4, and the [hydrogen phosphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphate "Phosphate") ion HPO2−4, respectively. Phosphoric acid forms [esters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esters "Esters"), called [organophosphates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organophosphate "Organophosphate").[[16]](#cite_note-Westheimer-16)

The name "orthophosphoric acid" can be used to distinguish this specific acid from other "[phosphoric acids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphoric_acids_and_phosphates "Phosphoric acids and phosphates")", such as [pyrophosphoric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrophosphoric_acid "Pyrophosphoric acid"). Nevertheless, the term "phosphoric acid" often means this specific compound; and that is the current [IUPAC nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUPAC_nomenclature "IUPAC nomenclature").

## Production

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Phosphoric_acid&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Production")]

Phosphoric acid is produced industrially by one of two routes, wet processes and dry.[[17]](#cite_note-17)[[18]](#cite_note-18)[[19]](#cite_note-19)

### Wet process

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Phosphoric_acid&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Wet process")]

In the wet process, phosphate-containing minerals such as calcium [hydroxyapatite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydroxyapatite "Hydroxyapatite") or [fluorapatite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluorapatite "Fluorapatite") are treated with [sulfuric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfuric_acid "Sulfuric acid").[[20]](#cite_note-20)

:   Ca5(PO4)3OH + 5 H2SO4 → 3 H3PO4 + 5 [CaSO4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CaSO4 "CaSO4") + H2O
:   Ca5(PO4)3F + 5 H2SO4 → 3 H3PO4 + 5 [CaSO4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CaSO4 "CaSO4") + HF

By-products include [calcium sulfate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calcium_sulfate "Calcium sulfate") (CaSO4) and [hydrogen fluoride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_fluoride "Hydrogen fluoride") (HF). The HF gas may be recovered by streaming it into a [wet (water) scrubber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wet_scrubber "Wet scrubber") producing [hydrofluoric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrofluoric_acid "Hydrofluoric acid"). CaSO4 is better known as gypsum, which is commonly used in the construction industry, however the CaSO4 produced from phosphoric acid production can contain trace levels of radioactive elements such as [radium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radium "Radium"). This makes it unsuitable for commercial use, and it is called [phosphogypsum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphogypsum "Phosphogypsum") to distinguish it. It is typically stored indefinitely.

In both cases the phosphoric acid solution usually contains 23–33% P2O5 (32–46% H3PO4). It may be concentrated to produce *commercial-* or *merchant-grade* phosphoric acid, which contains about 54–62% [P2O5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphorus_pentoxide "Phosphorus pentoxide") (75–85% H3PO4). Further removal of water yields *superphosphoric acid* with a P2O5 concentration above 70% (corresponding to nearly 100% H3PO4). The phosphoric acid from both processes may be further purified by removing compounds of arsenic and other potentially toxic impurities.

### Dry process

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Phosphoric_acid&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Dry process")]

To produce food-grade phosphoric acid, phosphate ore is first reduced with [coke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coke_(fuel) "Coke (fuel)") in an [electric arc furnace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_arc_furnace "Electric arc furnace"), to give elemental [phosphorus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphorus "Phosphorus"). This process is also known as the thermal process or the electric furnace process. Silica is also added, resulting in the production of [calcium silicate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calcium_silicate "Calcium silicate") slag. Elemental phosphorus is distilled out of the furnace and burned with air to produce high-purity [phosphorus pentoxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphorus_pentoxide "Phosphorus pentoxide"), which is dissolved in water to make phosphoric acid.[[21]](#cite_note-21) The thermal process produces phosphoric acid with a very high concentration of P2O5 (about 85%) and a low level of impurities.

However, this process is more expensive and energy-intensive than the wet process, which produces phosphoric acid with a lower concentration of P2O5 (about 26–52%) and a higher level of impurities. The wet process is the most common method of producing phosphoric acid for fertilizer use.[[22]](#cite_note-22) Even in China, where the thermal process is still used quite widely due to relatively cheap coal as opposed to the sulfuric acid, over 7/8 of phosphoric acid is produced with wet process.[[23]](#cite_note-23)

## Purification

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Phosphoric_acid&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Purification")]

Phosphoric acid produced from [phosphate rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphate_rock "Phosphate rock") or thermal processes often requires purification. A common purification method is [liquid–liquid extraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid–liquid_extraction "Liquid–liquid extraction"), which involves the separation of phosphoric acid from water and other impurities using organic solvents, such as [tributyl phosphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tributyl_phosphate "Tributyl phosphate") (TBP), [methyl isobutyl ketone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methyl_isobutyl_ketone "Methyl isobutyl ketone") (MIBK), or [*n*-octanol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N-octanol "N-octanol"). [Nanofiltration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanofiltration "Nanofiltration") involves the use of a premodified nanofiltration membrane, which is functionalized by a deposit of a high molecular weight polycationic [polymer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polymer "Polymer") of [polyethyleneimines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyethyleneamines "Polyethyleneamines"). Nanofiltration has been shown to significantly reduce the concentrations of various impurities, including [cadmium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadmium "Cadmium"), [aluminum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium "Aluminium"), [iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron "Iron"), and [rare earth elements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rare-earth_element "Rare-earth element"). The laboratory and industrial pilot scale results showed that this process allows the production of food-grade phosphoric acid.[[24]](#cite_note-24)

[Fractional crystallization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractional_crystallization_(chemistry) "Fractional crystallization (chemistry)") can achieve higher purities typically used for semiconductor applications. Usually a static crystallizer is used. A static crystallizer uses vertical plates, which are suspended in the molten feed and which are alternatingly cooled and heated by a heat transfer medium. The process begins with the slow cooling of the heat transfer medium below the freezing point of the stagnant melt. This cooling causes a layer of crystals to grow on the plates. Impurities are rejected from the growing crystals and are concentrated in the remaining melt. After the desired fraction has been crystallized, the remaining melt is drained from the crystallizer. The purer crystalline layer remains adhered to the plates. In a subsequent step, the plates are heated again to liquify the crystals and the purified phosphoric acid drained into the product vessel. The crystallizer is filled with feed again and the next cooling cycle is started.[[25]](#cite_note-25)

## Properties

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Phosphoric_acid&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Properties")]

### Acidic properties

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Phosphoric_acid&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Acidic properties")]

In aqueous solution phosphoric acid behaves as a triprotic acid.

:   H3PO4 ⇌ H2PO−4 + H+, p*K*a1 = 2.14
:   H2PO−4 ⇌ HPO2−4 + H+, p*K*a2 = 7.20
:   HPO2−4 ⇌ PO3−4 + H+, p*K*a3 = 12.37

The difference between successive [p*K*a](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PKa "PKa") values is sufficiently large so that salts of either monohydrogen phosphate, HPO2−4 or dihydrogen phosphate, H2PO−4, can be prepared from a solution of phosphoric acid by adjusting the [pH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PH "PH") to be mid-way between the respective p*K*a values.

### Aqueous solutions

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Phosphoric_acid&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Aqueous solutions")]

Aqueous solutions up to 62.5% H3PO4 are [eutectic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eutectic "Eutectic"), exhibiting freezing-point depression as low as −85 °C. When the concentration of acid rises above 62.5% the freezing-point increases, reaching 21 °C by 85% H3PO4 (w/w; the [monohydrate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monohydrate "Monohydrate")). Beyond this the [phase diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_diagram "Phase diagram") becomes complicated, with significant local maxima and minima. For this reason phosphoric acid is rarely sold above 85%, as beyond this adding or removing small amounts of moisture risks the entire mass freezing solid, which would be a major problem on a large scale. There exists a local maximum at 91.6% which corresponds to the [hemihydrate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hemihydrate "Hemihydrate") 2H3PO4•H2O, freezing at 29.32 °C.[[26]](#cite_note-26)[[27]](#cite_note-27) There is a second smaller eutectic depression at a concentration of 94.75% with a freezing point of 23.5 °C. At higher concentrations the freezing point rapidly increases. Concentrated phosphoric acid tends to [supercool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercooling "Supercooling") before crystallization occurs, and may be relatively resistant to crystallisation even when stored below the freezing point.[[4]](#cite_note-Ross-4)

### Self condensation

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Phosphoric_acid&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Self condensation")]

Phosphoric acid is commercially available as aqueous solutions of various concentrations, not usually exceeding 85%. If concentrated further it undergoes slow self-condensation, forming an equilibrium with [pyrophosphoric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrophosphoric_acid "Pyrophosphoric acid"):

:   2 H3PO4 ⇌ H2O + H4P2O7

Even at 90% concentration the amount of pyrophosphoric acid present is negligible, but beyond 95% it starts to increase, reaching 15% at what would have otherwise been 100% orthophosphoric acid.[[28]](#cite_note-28)

As the concentration is increased [higher acids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphoric_acids_and_phosphates "Phosphoric acids and phosphates") are formed, culminating in the formation of [polyphosphoric acids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyphosphoric_acid "Polyphosphoric acid").[[29]](#cite_note-29) It is not possible to fully dehydrate phosphoric acid to [phosphorus pentoxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphorus_pentoxide "Phosphorus pentoxide"), instead the polyphosphoric acid becomes increasingly polymeric and viscous. Due to the self-condensation, pure orthophosphoric acid can only be obtained by a careful fractional freezing/melting process.[[4]](#cite_note-Ross-4)[[3]](#cite_note-Greenwood-3)

## Uses

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Phosphoric_acid&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Uses")]

The dominant use of phosphoric acid is for [fertilizers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fertilizer "Fertilizer"), consuming approximately 90% of production.[[30]](#cite_note-Ullmann-30)

The remaining 10% is primarily used in soaps and detergents:

Food-grade phosphoric acid (additive [E338](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E_number "E number")[[31]](#cite_note-fgovuk-31)) is used to acidify foods and beverages such as various [colas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cola "Cola") and jams, providing a tangy or sour taste. The phosphoric acid also serves as a [preservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preservative "Preservative").[[32]](#cite_note-32) Soft drinks containing phosphoric acid, which would include [Coca-Cola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coca-Cola "Coca-Cola"), are sometimes called [phosphate sodas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphate_soda "Phosphate soda") or phosphates. Phosphoric acid in soft drinks has the potential to cause dental erosion.[[33]](#cite_note-33) Phosphoric acid also has the potential to contribute to the formation of [kidney stones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kidney_stone_disease "Kidney stone disease"), especially in those who have had kidney stones previously.[[34]](#cite_note-Qa2014-34)

Specific applications of phosphoric acid include:

* in anti-rust ([iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron "Iron") and [steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steel "Steel") [oxidation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxidation "Oxidation")) treatment by [phosphate conversion coating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphate_conversion_coating "Phosphate conversion coating") or [passivation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passivation_(chemistry) "Passivation (chemistry)"),[[35]](#cite_note-35) including the [Parkerization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parkerization_(metallurgy) "Parkerization (metallurgy)") process
* as an external standard for [phosphorus-31 nuclear magnetic resonance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphorus-31_nuclear_magnetic_resonance "Phosphorus-31 nuclear magnetic resonance")
* in [phosphoric acid fuel cells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphoric_acid_fuel_cell "Phosphoric acid fuel cell")
* in [activated carbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Activated_carbon "Activated carbon") production[[36]](#cite_note-36)
* in [compound semiconductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compound_semiconductor "Compound semiconductor") processing, to etch [Indium gallium arsenide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indium_gallium_arsenide "Indium gallium arsenide") selectively with respect to [indium phosphide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indium_phosphide "Indium phosphide")[[37]](#cite_note-37)
* in [microfabrication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microfabrication "Microfabrication") to etch [silicon nitride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_nitride "Silicon nitride") selectively with respect to [silicon dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_dioxide "Silicon dioxide")[[38]](#cite_note-Wolf-38)
* in microfabrication to etch [aluminium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium "Aluminium")
* as a pH adjuster in cosmetics and skin-care products[[39]](#cite_note-39)
* as a sanitizing agent in the dairy, food, and brewing industries[[40]](#cite_note-40)
* in [chemical polishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical-mechanical_polishing "Chemical-mechanical polishing") ([etching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etching "Etching")) of metals like aluminium

## Safety

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Phosphoric_acid&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Safety")]

Phosphoric acid is not a [strong acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_acid "Strong acid"). However, at moderate concentrations phosphoric acid solutions are irritating to the skin. Contact with concentrated solutions can cause severe skin burns and permanent eye damage.[[41]](#cite_note-:0-41)

**1. Sustainable & Circular Production**

The industrial phosphoric acid market is seeing a shift towards circular and sustainable manufacturing that emphasises resource efficiency and waste reduction. At a rate of 4–6 tonnes every tonne of PA produced, phosphogypsum is a substantial by-product of PA manufacturing. A circular economy is being promoted by the repurposing of PG, which was once dumped, in a variety of uses, such as mine repair, cement, and plaster. Furthermore, to further advance sustainability, novel techniques are being created to extract important materials from PG, including rare earth elements. In addition to lessening their influence on the environment, these programs support international sustainability objectives.

**2. Mergers, Acquisitions & Strategic Partnerships**

The industrial phosphoric acid industry is significantly shaped by mergers, acquisitions, and strategic alliances. In an effort to improve their operational efficiency and market visibility, businesses are merging more frequently. For example, The Mosaic Company increased its upstream supply capacity by purchasing a regional phosphate rock mining operator. Similarly, Nutrien and Yara International established a joint venture in North America to produce green phosphate using renewable energy. By securing feedstock, increasing their regional footprint, and incorporating sustainable manufacturing practices, these strategic actions help businesses maintain a competitive edge in the changing market environment.

**3. Technological Advancements in Production Processes**

Efficiency and purity in the manufacturing of phosphoric acid are being improved by technological developments. Improved separation and concentration stages, lower energy consumption, and less contamination hazards are all benefits of membrane filtering technologies, which are essential for applications such as semiconductors. Accurate control over production parameters is made possible by automation and real-time monitoring technologies, such as smart sensors and AI-driven analytics, which guarantee that the acid satisfies the strict purity requirements needed for semiconductor manufacture. Phosphoric acid production methods are changing as a result of these advancements, especially in sectors where high purity is crucial.

**4. Grade and Application Diversification**

The market for industrial phosphoric acid is diversifying significantly in terms of grade and application due to changing industrial demands and technological breakthroughs. Even while technical grade phosphoric acid is still widely used, its proportion is steadily declining as demand for higher-purity grades rises. Food-grade phosphoric acid is steadily increasing in use as a preservative and acidity regulator in processed foods and beverages. At the same time, the electronics industry is becoming a significant user, employing electronic-grade phosphoric acid in precision etching and semiconductor production. Phosphoric acid's versatility across a range of industries is demonstrated by this diversification, underscoring its crucial significance beyond conventional applications.

**5. Environmental Regulation & Carbon Footprint Pressure**

Pressures related to the carbon footprint and environmental requirements are having a big impact on the industrial phosphoric acid sector. PA manufacturing uses a lot of energy and produces a lot of carbon emissions, especially when done the old-fashioned wet way. For example, a standard facility that can produce one million tonnes of PA annually can emit. Stricter environmental standards are being enforced by regulatory frameworks, particularly in North America and Europe, to lessen these effects. According to Global Growth Insights, manufacturers must lower their carbon footprints and embrace cleaner technology, which will raise manufacturing costs. The industry is moving towards more innovative production methods and environmental practices as a result of these rules.

* Product Purity: The level of impurities impacts downstream applications, especially in food and electronics.
* Production Capacity: Larger capacities can meet bulk demands but may sacrifice flexibility.
* Cost Efficiency: Competitive pricing without compromising quality is vital for cost-sensitive buyers.
* Supply Chain Reliability: Consistent delivery schedules and geographic reach reduce risks.
* Technological Innovation: Advanced production methods can enhance purity and reduce environmental impact.
* Environmental & Safety Standards: Compliance with regulations minimizes legal and reputational risks.
* Customer Support & Service: Technical assistance and after-sales support influence long-term partnerships.
* Financial Stability: Stable vendors are better positioned to invest in R&D and capacity expansion.

Phosphoric Acid is used in a wide array of applications including the manufacturing of phosphate salts. Purified phosphoric acid is a high-quality, versatile chemical essential for numerous industries.   
   
 As a leading specialty phosphate manufacturer, Innophos delivers the highest purity standards, making it ideal for food, beverage, pharmaceutical applications and lithium-ion battery materials. Our North American production facilities meet [stringent safety and regulatory requirements](/customer-center/plant-certificates) providing security and proximity of supply for regional manufacturers.   
   
 In addition to being a chemical reagent, [Phosphoric Acid Food Grade](/products/phos-acid-food) is used as an ingredient in foods and beverages to enhance flavors and act as a preservative. Phosphoric Acid is typically used for pH control in the food industry, for example in the manufacture of cheese products, fats, and shortenings. It is also used in the beverage industry in soft drinks, particularly cola.   
   
 [Phosphoric Acid Tech Grade](/products/phos-acid-tech) is used in plant nutrition applications to provide precise and targeted fortification with water-soluble solutions. Phosphoric Acid is also used for water treatment, metal finishing, construction, and other industrial applications.  
   
 [Phosphoric Acid (Battery Grade)](/products/voltix-phos-acid-battery) is used in lithium-ion batteries as a key phosphorus source in the synthesis of phosphate-based cathodes of lithium iron phosphate (LFP), lithium manganese iron phosphate (LMFP) and for electrolyte salts, lithium hexafluorophosphate (LiPF6).

## How Innophos Processes Purified Phosphoric Acid

Innophos processes phosphoric acid through a series of advanced chemical engineering steps, ensuring high purity and consistency for its various applications. The typical process includes the following steps:  
   
 **1. Raw Material Selection:** Innophos sources phosphate rock, a natural mineral, as the primary raw material.  
   
 **2. Acidulation:**After being shipped to a manufacturing facility, the phosphate rock undergoes processing with sulfuric acid in large reactors, producing phosphoric acid. This process is known as the wet-process method. The wet process is favored due to its lower energy consumption and cost-effectiveness.  
   
 **3. Purification:** After the initial phosphoric acid is created, it then goes through a process to remove impurities. This process involves filtration and chemical treatments to ensure the final product meets specific purity standards required for different applications, such as food, technical, or industrial grades.  
   
 **4. Concentration:** The purified phosphoric acid is concentrated through evaporation. This step increases the acid's concentration to desired levels, usually around 75% to 85% H3PO4 for various industrial and food-grade uses.  
   
 **5. Quality:**Throughout the process, Innophos employs stringent quality and food safety control measures, including regular testing and analysis, to ensure the product meets the necessary specifications and regulatory requirements. For food grade products, [our manufacturing operations](/who-we-are/about-us/manufacturing-capabilities) meet Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP), and [all manufacturing sites](/who-we-are/about-us/our-locations) have Global Food Safety Initiative (GFSI) certification. Additionally, Innophos has robust preventive controls in place to meet the requirements of the Food Safety Modernization Act (FSMA).  
   
 **6. Packaging and Distribution:**The final phosphoric acid product is then packaged in appropriate containers, ranging from bulk tanks for industrial use to smaller containers for food-grade applications, and distributed to customers.  
   
 These steps ensure that Innophos provides high-quality phosphoric acid suitable for a range of uses, from food & beverage or other industrial applications.
